## Chapter 43.

<margin>Chapter 43.</margin>
# Concerning the Destruction of *Sodom* and *Gomorra*, and how *God* indicated it to *Abraham* beforehand.

<margin>Genesis 18. 19. 20.</margin>

And the *Lord* spoke to *Abraham*, after He had blessed *Abraham* and said how He would command his children to walk in the ways of the *Lord*, and how He would bless them accordingly, as was explained earlier: "Behold, the cry of *Sodom* and *Gomorra* is great, and their sins are very heavy; therefore *I* will go down and see whether they have done everything according to the cry that has come before me, or whether it is not so, so that *I* may know." And the men turned their faces and went toward *Sodom*. *God* spoke: "How can I hide from *Abraham* what I am doing, since he is to become a great nation?" and He indicated to him what He intended to do.

2. Unenlightened reason <term>Vernunfft (the human faculty of rational but limited understanding)</term> looks upon this figure <note>original: "Figur" — a symbolic representation or biblical scene</note> strangely—that *God* said He would go down and see if the outcry were true so that He might know it, and whether it was so or not. For reason thinks: "Is He then localized, or only Above? Does He not already know everything beforehand?" especially since the Scripture says of Him: "Is it not *I* who fills all things?" Also: "Heaven is my throne, and the earth is my footstool." Would He then first have to travel down like a localized being <note>original: "mäßiglichen Wesen" — a limited or measurable being</note> that is separated by time and place?

3. Rather, that "cry" which came up before Him is unfathomable to reason. For these reasons, creaturely reason thinks *God* dwells alone Above, beyond the stars in a separate heaven, and looks down from there just as the sun’s radiance looks and shines from its body upon the earth. Thus far has reason come; it knows no more of what *God* is or where *God* is. It does not know that He is all Essence <term>Wesen (Being, substance, or the essential reality of things)</term>, and dwells through all essence, and occupies no fixed place, nor needs any spot or space for a dwelling. It does not know that He—insofar as He is called *God*—is no "thing" or essence, but compared to essence, He is like a "Nothing" <note>This refers to the author's concept of the "Ungrund," the divine nothingness or abyss out of which all existence flows.</note>. Yet He is through Everything, and gives Himself over to the essence as a working force, just as the power of the sun works in fruit—not from the outside in, but working from the inside out toward His own revelation within the creature and its life. Nature and the creature are His revelation; if reason understood this rightly, it would have no further questions here.

<summary>Abraham is informed by God of the impending judgment on Sodom and Gomorrah, prompting a mystical discussion on God's nature. The author explains that God is not a distant, localized judge, but an omnipresent essence working from within all of creation.</summary>

<margin>¶</margin>4. Understand the meaning in this way: God dwells in Himself, according to both Love and Wrath; each property looks only into itself, and is not manifest in the other with its own property, just as you have a comparison in day and night, or in light and darkness; the light dwells in the darkness and sees it not: Likewise, the darkness does not see the light, and just as the light dwells in its great gentleness within the fire, and yet does not take the fire's torment and pain upon itself, but remains good alone, without a felt life of the fire; and yet it originates <note>original: "vhrständet" — to arise or take a stand from a source</note> through the consuming of the fire, as through the dying of the being: Understand the Being of God in this same way.

5. God’s Eye of Love does not look <term>essentially (in its true inner substance)</term> <note>original: "Essentialiter"</note> into the malicious, turned-away soul, nor likewise into the Devil; rather, His Eye of Wrath looks into them—that is, according to the property of Wrath or Fire-Fierceness, God sees into the Devil and into the false soul.

6. Therefore God said: An outcry had come before Him; by this He meant His revealed Word, as the voice in the divine revealed <term>being (the inner substance of a thing)</term> <note>original: "Ente"</note> of these three men; it had come before the <term>essence (the core reality)</term> <note>original: "Ens"</note> and before the Hearing that had presented itself in the promised <term>being</term> <note>original: "Ente"</note>, the human becoming the humanity of Christ, now in Three Persons.

7. For to this Word or Hearing, the judgment over all Devils and godless men had been given; for that was the mobile Hearing, through which God the Father heard into humanity, and through which He willed to separate the evil from the good.

8. Thus this Hearing—as the Hearing that willed to manifest itself in humanity in the Person of Christ—had the voice of the Sodomites, as the children of Ham <note>In the biblical tradition, the descendants of Ham were often associated with those who turned away from God's path</note>, within itself; that is, it heard according to the property of Wrath, and brought that hearing before the infinite Hearing into the first <term>Principle (the foundational source of nature)</term> <note>original: "Principium"</note>, as into the origin of nature and the creature: For the Sodomites, as children of the flesh, live alone in the hearing of this world, as in the outspoken formed Word, in the figure of the Deity, where evil and good are manifest together in one being.

10. Thus the outcry of the Sodomites had come "Above"—arriving at the first <term>Principle (the fundamental source of reality)</term>, where the "Above" emerges from the Nothingness into the first eternal beginning, taking shape as a nature and a formation of the powers or the Word. God’s "grasped" or "conceived" Word—His voice emerging from the property of the Father and the Son, and from God's love and wrath (which had promised itself to humanity as a future Christ, contained within a divine <term>Ens (a spiritual substance or essence)</term>)—had heard the outcry within the property of Wrath, through which He acts as a judge of all ungodly existence.

11. So the Father spoke: "I will go down to see if it is so." This means that with that same contained "hearing" of these three men <note>The "three men" are the visitors to Abraham, traditionally interpreted as angels or a manifestation of the Trinity</note> within the <term>Ens</term>—which God had formed to be the Judge of the world, and who was to become Christ—He came down; that is, He emerged from the "Above."

12. For that same <term>Ens</term> was to exist as a creature in a Person; therefore, within the grasped Word of the Promise, it was formally shaped in the manner of an angel. In this way, He came from above—that is, out of the "Above," which is God, the immutable God. He first heard within Abraham, within the <term>Ens</term> of the Covenant, reaching the goal of His Covenant with both His love and His wrath. Just as one hears through the medium of fire, He hears the malice and vanity of humanity. He saw with the Eye of Wrath what they were doing; that is, His fury looked <term>essentially (into the core substance)</term> <note>original: "Essentialiter"</note> into human vanity and malice. This occurred in the same way that a <term>murderous fire</term> <margin>smolders</margin> within wood and seeks to consume it. Thus God, with His eye of wrath within the formed <term>being (the inner substance)</term> <note>original: "Ente"</note>, looked through that same Word of Judgment in Christ’s <term>being</term>—by which He will judge the world—into the ungodly serpent-malice and the will of the children of Ham in Sodom and Gomorrah.

13. For just as God presented to Himself in Abraham the new birth of His holy children out of His <term>being</term> of love, He also presented to Himself the judgment within His <term>being</term> of wrath, showing how He intended to test the ungodly by fire through this Christ.

14. And the judgment over Sodom is a <term>figure (a symbolic precursor or type)</term> of the Final Judgment. Just as the three men before Abraham were a figure of our new "angelic" humanity, where God dwells in man, so too His wrath dwells in the ungodly. Here we see how God intends to judge the devils and all ungodly people through the "children of the holy." This is mirrored here as He presents the figure of the judicial office in a threefold humanity and wipes Sodom and Gomorrah from the world.

15. God also said to Abraham: "How can I hide from Abraham what I am doing?" To the earthly Abraham, it would have been hidden; but from the heavenly Abraham—born of God’s <term>Ens</term>—God did not wish to conceal it. Here God presented the figure of His love and His wrath as the humanity of Christ.

# On the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah!

### How God led Abraham so wonderfully, and how he was always standing in temptation, and how the Lord shielded him: what is to be understood by this.

Abraham had to be <gloss>as</gloss> a pilgrim on Earth, and move from one place to another and dwell in tents, and was tested everywhere; as his wife Sarah was taken from him twice, but was wonderfully shielded and preserved by God—once by Pharaoh in Egypt, and by Abimelech, King of Gerar—but both times he was shielded by God.

2. And that Abraham, as the stem and beginning of the conceived faith, of the <term>Being</term> <note>original: "Entis." Latin for "of a being" or "essence." An archetypal pattern or prophetic model.</note> of Christendom on Earth, showing how it would not be bound to any certain place; not to one people alone, whom God had chosen especially for that purpose, but that Christ with his Gospel of the Kingdom of God has been given to all nations.

# How God led Abraham so miraculously, etc.

<margin><unclear>Gen. 12.</unclear></margin>
16. For he cannot endure by himself; only Christ within him must be his courage and his constancy. Just as Abraham was doubtful in his own strength before Pharaoh and Abimelech <note>Abraham twice claimed his wife Sarah was his sister out of fear for his life, once in Egypt (Genesis 12) and once in Gerar (Genesis 20).</note>, and was always fearful for his life, he had to see how God protected both him and his Sarah. This history is described so masterfully and precisely regarding the Kingdom of Christ—from the <term>Esraim vision</term> <note>original: "Esraim Gesichte"; likely a reference to a prophetic or spiritual perspective associated with Ephraim or the visionary Esra, signifying a deep spiritual insight into the future.</note> of the Spirit of Christ—as if the Spirit purposefully shaped these stories to prefigure the Kingdom of Christ, for it is entirely directed toward that.

17. For the <term>outer man</term> <note>The physical, worldly aspect of a person, as opposed to the "inner" spiritual soul.</note> understands nothing at all of the Kingdom of Christ, as can be seen with Sarah. When she became pregnant and gave birth to Isaac, she said, "The Lord has prepared a laugh for me" <note>Genesis 21:6. The name Isaac means "he laughs."</note>—that is, people will laugh that the old, ninety-year-old Sarah is nursing a child. She did not yet understand the **Image of Christ** <note>The idea that Isaac's miraculous birth was a "type" or preview of Christ's birth.</note>; rather, the Spirit of Christ within her understood it. It was not the natural man in his <term>selfhood</term> <note>original: "selbheit"; the state of being focused on one's own ego and desires rather than God's will.</note>, but the **resigned will**, which was surrendered into God; that will alone grasped the Covenant and the Spirit of Christ.

18. But **Reason**, as the self-centered will, stood mute before it; to it, the matter was merely a "laugh," for it looked only upon itself and what it was. Just as Abraham’s will in his own selfhood looked only upon himself and was terrified—even though within him was the great power over all authority and dominions—that power did not belong to **human selfhood**.

19. In the same way, Christ in His children does not belong to the human selfhood or the self-centered will; He does not make Himself a part of it. Rather, He joins Himself to the **humble, resigned will** <note>original: "gelassenen Willen"; a central term in German mysticism referring to "Gelassenheit," the state of letting go of one's own will to let God act.</note>; He makes Himself one with that, and thereby often protects the "own will" as well.

20. For the "own will" is of the nature of this world, made of flesh and blood. But the **resigned will** dies to the world and is born into life in God. Thus, we are to understand two kinds of wills in Abraham and in all Christians: one from this world, which stands forever in fear; and then the will of the poor, captive soul according to the <term>Second Principle</term> <note>In the author's theology, the "Second Principle" is the world of light, love, and the Kingdom of Heaven.</note>, which is directed toward the Kingdom of Heaven, and which

## The 46th Chapter.

# Of Isaac’s Birth and Ishmael’s Expulsion, with his Mother Hagar, and what is signified thereby.

->Genesis 21<-

The Spirit in Moses sets forth the **pattern of man’s rebirth** <note>original: "Figur des Menschen Wiedergeburth"; the author views biblical events as "figures" or "types" representing the internal process of a soul being born again in Christ.</note> in its progression so precisely and orderly in the history of Abraham, that one could almost grasp it, let alone see it. He places the natural man in his selfhood and Christ side by side, and points to the pattern as if with his fingers: For when God had destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah—the region where Abraham dwelt—and led Lot out, Abraham moved from there toward the south <note>original: "gegen Mittag," literally "toward noon," a common early modern term for the South.</note>. This signifies that when the Kingdom of Christ is corrupted in one place, Christ will depart from it; thus Abraham betook himself under King Abimelech and became a stranger at Gerar.

2. In these two names, Abimelech and Gerar, the pattern stands in the generation or conception of the Word without any forced interpretation. One can see through it as if through a looking-glass why the Spirit in Moses wrote down this very history: For **Abimelech** signifies the man of sensory reason—as the true man, but outside of Christ, existing only in the creaturely state as he was created. **Gerar** signifies the harsh life of nature in which the understanding must dwell. This nature is corrupted, and from its corruption, it constantly throws **temptation** <note>original: "Anfechtung"; a specific term for spiritual trials or "assaults" from the devil or one's own nature.</note> and adversity into the understanding of life or the "Light of Reason." Thus, life stands in constant adversity and is incessantly sifted and tried <note>original: "gefeyet," meaning to be purified as if by fire.</note>. This is the "cross of the children of God": they see that when they live in themselves and in their own reason, they cannot help but stumble and err. We see this here with Abraham: when God led him away from the borders of the Sodomites, he moved toward the south to King Abimelech.

->This pattern stands internally as follows:<-

3. When God had revealed Himself to Abraham and presented the pattern of Christ and His Kingdom, along with the power of judgment over the world, God hid Himself again from Abraham. Then Abraham went toward the south—that is, into his **reason**, into man’s own understanding—and dwelt at Gerar. This represents dwelling in corrupted nature, which is demonstrated in the history with Abimelech: there, out of the fear of nature during temptation, he denied his wife, claiming she was not his wife, so that he might

# Of Isaac’s Birth and Ishmael’s Expulsion /

<margin>76. a. +</margin>...might seek to preserve through the cunning of **Reason** <term>Vernunfft: In this mystical context, it refers to the limited, earthly human intellect that often lacks faith and acts out of self-preservation.</term>, and one sees quite clearly how that very thing from which he thought to protect himself in his Reason, had to punish and teach him. For Abimelech rebuked him because he had denied his wife—an act through which he had almost led Abimelech into sin, had the Lord not warned him. And the explanation of this is:

4. When one sees a person whom the **Spirit of God** drives, and through whom the Spirit often speaks, one should not fall into the trap of thinking he is something different from other men. For Abraham was also nothing else; the personal Reason within him was just as wavering and imperfect as it is in other men. That which they know and teach of God is not their own property at all, as is seen here in Abraham. Even out of fear for his Sarah—whom he denied out of fear—he did not spare her, even though Abimelech might have taken her from him as a concubine <note>original: "Kebsweibe"</note>, simply so that he might live and that things might go better for him for her sake.

5. In this way, God proves <note>original: "probieret"; to test or put through a trial to reveal the true nature of a substance or soul.</note> His children, so that they may see that in their own power they are nothing more than all other sinful men, and so that one should not rely on men or hold them for God. Thus, God also lets them often stumble and err, and then lets them be rebuked even by those whom they themselves should teach. This is seen here in Abimelech, how he had to rebuke Abraham and make him blush with shame, because for the sake of a small fear he did not spare his wife and denied her.

<note>A decorative bracket with a pointing hand indicates the start of paragraph 6.</note>
6. And should it happen that one sees such a person—whom God nevertheless drives—err at times, one should not immediately cast him away and think he is entirely outside of God, as the world does. Rather, one should think that God thus places His children into the trial <note>original: "Proba"</note> under the **Cross** <term>Creutz: A central concept representing the suffering and refinement necessary to die to the self and be reborn in God.</term>, so they may learn to know themselves. Then the sun rises for them again, as it did here for Abraham when God let him travel toward Gerar—that is, into his natural, rational life, wherein he stumbled before Abimelech. Afterward, a twofold Sun rose for him: One, that Abimelech recognized him and learned to fear the Lord, giving Abraham the land for a dwelling and giving him gifts as a punishment—just as one punishes the Saints when one fears God’s punishment. Thus the Sun of Grace of King Abimelech rose for him. And then, secondly, Sarah became pregnant, and a Branch came forth for him out of the **Line of the Covenant** <note>original: "Bundes-Linea"; the spiritual lineage through which the Promised Seed, or Christ, would eventually manifest.</note>, out of the Divine Solar Power, and Isaac was born to him.

### with his mother Hagar / what is signified thereby. ###

<margin>46. Chapter <note>This likely refers to the chapter numbering of the author's specific commentary rather than a biblical chapter.</note></margin>
7. And so that one may understand this correctly, the **Cross** always stands by the children of God, and **Adam** and **Christ** are ever present with one another—just as here Abimelech and Abraham, and Ishmael and Isaac are paired. So too the person of **Reason** <term>Vernunfft: In this mystical context, Reason refers to the limited human intellect that relies on its own logic rather than divine revelation.</term> and the corrupt nature stand against that higher Reason, which the spiritual Reason sifts without ceasing. This can also be seen here with Hagar and Sarah, who were set against one another so that one might exercise the other: Hagar in the quality <note>original: "Eigenschafft"</note> of the corrupt nature, as in Adam’s life, and Sarah in Christ’s person, so that Hagar might exercise the natural Sarah, driving her out of human Reason and into God.

8. In Sarah and her maid Hagar—with her son Ishmael and with Isaac, Sarah’s son—and in how Sarah cast out the maid with her son (which displeased Abraham but was right before God), we have such a mirror as is not found elsewhere in the Bible. It shows how Christ and the natural man dwell together, and how the natural man must be entirely cast out with Ishmael and his mother from **Inheritance-Righteousness** <term>Erb-Gerechtigkeit: The mistaken belief that one can inherit God’s favor through natural birth or personal merit rather than through spiritual rebirth.</term> and the "own-will," for the natural self-will is no heir of God.

9. And when the **resigned will** <term>gelassene Wille: A key concept in German mysticism (Gelassenheit), referring to a soul that has surrendered all selfish desires and "let go" to God’s will.</term> has cast them out, then the poor nature of man sits with its rejected will in trembling and prepares to die—just as Hagar did here with her son Ishmael. When she had been cast out by Abraham, she went into the wilderness of **Beersheba** <note>original: "Bersaba"</note>, which is to say, into the brokenness <note>original: "zerborstigkeit"</note> of her heart. She saw herself entirely abandoned and despaired of her life and her son’s life, being powerless. For they had lost their inheritance, as well as the favor of the Mistress and all goods; now there was neither water nor bread for life, and they were surrendered to death. For she placed herself a stone’s throw away from the boy so that she would not have to see him die. And as she had now entirely surrendered herself to death, the Angel came to her again and called to her and comforted her; he also showed her a well and told her she should not tremble unto death, for her son must yet become a great nation.

-> This figure is represented internally as follows <-

10. When Isaac, that is **Christ**, is born in the converted person, then the spiritual, newborn will rejects its own evil nature. It despises it and judges it to death; it also thrusts it out of itself along with its son, the **Mocker** <note>original: "Spötter"</note> or the "Wrong-Interpreter." It is as if the mind would burst apart, so angry does the newborn spiritual will become at the natural will and its "evil virtues"—represented by Ishmael, the son of the natural will, who is merely a mocker, liar, slanderer, and an unjust one.

Arise / that is / lift yourself up in God in this yieldedness <term>Gelassenheit: a central concept in German mysticism referring to the state of letting go of self-will and surrendering to God.</term> / and arise in the voice of being heard / and take your senses / as your son by the hand of faith / and lead the senses: They shall not die / but live and go / for I will make them into a great nation / that is / into a great divine understanding and comprehension of divine mysteries; and God opens to nature the wellspring of living water / so that she may receive from God's little fountain into the bottle of her being within herself / and with it gives the boy / as the senses / to drink.

# The 47th Chapter.
## Of the Covenant between Abimelech and Abraham: its meaning in the Spiritual Figure, and what the Spirit of Moses suggests here beneath its veil.

->Genesis 21<-

### A most noble and beautiful gateway for the children of God in Beersheba.

Dear reader, know this: even if one wrote many hundreds of books about the story of Abraham, one could never sufficiently express the richness hidden beneath this <term>Figur: a symbolic type or prefiguration</term>. However, we wish to perform a service for the children of God in their weakness and uncover this figure a little; for otherwise, it remains misunderstood by the <term>natürlichen Menschen: the "natural man" or person lacking spiritual insight</term>. But since the Lord leads us thus in grace, I shall here lend and give Him my hand. Take good note: there lies a pearl beneath it, which shall here stand open and yet also remain hidden—a pearl that cannot be paid for with all the world’s goods.

->The external figure stands thus in the text of Moses.<-

2. At that same time, Abimelech and Phichol, his army commander, spoke with Abraham, saying: "God is with you in everything you do; now swear to me by God that you will show no faithlessness to me, nor to my children, nor to my descendants, but that you will show the same kindness to me that I have shown to you, and to the land in which you are a stranger." Then Abraham said, "I will swear." And Abraham reproached Abimelech because of the water well which Abimelech's servants had seized by force. Then Abimelech answered: "I did not know who had done this, nor did you tell me, nor did I hear of it until today." Then Abraham took sheep and cattle and gave them to Abimelech, and they made a covenant with one another; and Abraham set seven lambs apart. Then Abimelech said to Abraham: "What are these seven lambs that you have set apart?" But he answered: "You shall take these seven lambs from my hand, so that they may be a witness for me that I dug this well." Therefore the place is called Beersheba <note>original: "Bersaba," meaning "Well of the Oath" or "Well of the Seven"</note>, because they both swore an oath there to one another; and so they made the covenant at Beersheba. Then Abimelech and Phichol his commander arose and moved back into the land of the Philistines, and—

Abraham planted trees at <note>original: "Bersaba"</note> Beersheba and preached there in the name of the Lord, the Eternal God, and was a stranger in the land of the Philistines for a long time. This <term>figure: a symbolic type or prefiguration</term> appears externally as if Abimelech had feared Abraham because God had given him to understand in a vision that Abraham was a prince of God; for this reason, he desired a covenant and oath from Abraham, so that Abraham would not perhaps destroy him and his descendants.

3. But the Spirit of Christ under the <note>original: "Moysis Deckel"</note> veil of Moses has painted here quite a different figure, with which he played and prophesied. For among all the histories of Abraham which the Spirit of Moses has written down, a twofold figure is set before us: to be understood as an external history of what once happened, and beneath that same history, the Spirit of Christ sets forth his figure in the covenant so gracefully, as if he were playing with it.

4. For that is precisely the place indicated where Hagar fled with Ishmael; it is the same Beersheba and the same well of water indicated which the angel showed to Hagar, which Abraham—that is, Christ—had dug. 5. And the covenant with Abimelech and Abraham is the covenant of Christ with humanity, where Abraham—that is, Christ—swore he would not destroy humanity; as he then said when he came into the flesh, that he had not come into this world to judge the world, but to make the world blessed—that is, to bless it and keep the covenant.

->The inner holy figure looks thus.<-

6. Abimelech and Phichol, who had spoken with Abraham concerning the covenant, are presented here by the Spirit as images of God the Father and of Nature. Abimelech the King indicates the Father in the <term>property: a specific quality or inner characteristic</term> of the Soul, and Phichol his army commander indicates Nature as God’s steward. These two approach the image of Christ as they approach Abraham; for to this Christ, all people had been given, for he was to be a Prince of God in and over humanity.

7. Now Nature had led itself from the Father’s property into false desire—understand this as human nature—for it desired to reveal Sarah as the Free One—understand this as the heavenly virginal <term>matrix: the spiritual womb or source of life</term>—within the earthly, beast-like property; this happened in Adam when he introduced his feminine property into a beast-like desire. Thus the Spirit in Moses points here to the same figure and presents Adam in the Father’s property and nature under the figure of King Abimelech.

...nor to my progeny <note>original: "Nesen," an archaic term for nephews or descendants</note> show any untruth, but rather show the mercy that I have shown to you, to me as well, and to the land wherein you are a stranger. This is as much as to say: it is as if God the Father in the soul were speaking with Christ His Son—to whom He had given all of humanity as His own property—and saying: "Since I have given you authority over human property (which is mine) as your own, now swear to me by God." That is, immerse yourself in an **Essential Oath** <note>an oath involving one’s very being or essence</note> or an Eternal Covenant, so that you will show no untruth to my nature in its human property, nor to the children (as the beings born anew out of their property), nor to their great-grandchildren or progeny. This refers to those in the "wild property"—where often a godless man and a godless woman mingle together, or where one is godless and the other is pious—meaning their children. Instead, you shall show the mercy that I have shown to you (in that I have given back to you this **Heavenly Matrix** <term>Matrix: the divine creative "womb" or "mother" of all things</term>, which in Adam was taken captive in my grimness and which faded away from your image in my wrath). You shall also show this mercy to your image and to the land—that is, to the external man, in whom God’s children carry the heavenly image—which is the land where you are a stranger.

13. For Christ is a stranger in our earthly humanity, and our earthly humanity often makes our children or progeny strangers to God. Therefore, the "Father of Nature" in the property of the soul said to Christ that He was a stranger in our land; just as Christ also said that His kingdom was not of this world—that is, not of the earthly man. However, Christ was to perform mercy in this foreign land (meaning foreign humanity) and not cast out the children born therein, just as the Father had done for His image of heavenly humanity, which had faded in Adam. Christ was to swear this in God, as He then swears in the prophet Ezekiel: *As truly as I live, I do not desire, nor do I have pleasure in the death of the godless or the sinner, but rather that he should convert and live.* For Abraham, acting as the figure of Christ, spoke: "I will swear"—that is, "I will do it."

14. And Abraham reproved Abimelech because of the water-well, which Abimelech’s servants had taken by force. That is: Christ reproved the soul, because the soul's servants—being the essences of nature—had taken the wellspring of the essence from the heavenly corporality (the body of Christ in Adam), from which the heavenly image died or faded away. For in the soul’s fiery essence, Christ’s holy little wellspring gushes forth; but the soul's essence had [taken] this well of divine **sweetness**—

# On the Birth of Isaac and the Expulsion of Ishmael

...and said: "What purpose do your **seven properties** <term>seven properties: Böhme’s central concept of the seven "qualities" or "source-spirits" that constitute both the divine nature and the human soul.</term> of our Divine Nature serve individually? Why? Because you are to give new birth to humans and dwell within them: Do you also wish to represent your **seven properties** of our Divine Nature in a specific Human Person?" And Christ answers in the figure of Abraham: "You shall take seven lambs from my hand, that they may be an eternal witness to me that I have dug this well." This is as much as to say: Christ speaks to his Father in a Human Person: "You shall take the figure or the image of my seven properties of the human creature as an eternal witness, that I have dug again the **wellspring** of Eternal Life through my suffering and death within the human property, so that the newly-dug human fountain of life is mine."

20. And the Spirit in Moses speaks quite covertly: "Therefore, or for this reason, the place is called **Beersheba**," <note>original: "Bersaba." Böhme interprets the name Beersheba through mystical wordplay, linking "Sheba" to the German word *zerschellen*, meaning to shatter or burst.</note> where they both swore an oath to one another; and thus they made the covenant at Beersheba. This is the most precious place, where God the Father and his Son in humanity swore an oath together. The place is called Beersheba, signifying a **shattering** of death at the fountain of the living and seeing one within faded humanity, where in Christ’s humanity—which he had taken from us humans—death was shattered and burst asunder. [It is] a Covenant, the fountain of love from the living God, returning into our shattered humanity’s heavenly part, back into the soul’s creaturely source. <margin>quality / source</margin> <note>original: "qual." In Böhme's terminology, this refers to the "Qual-ität" or the driving, stinging force of a property.</note> Thus the Spirit of Moses says here very finely that this place is called Beersheba, where the testimony of this oath was established as a fountain of grace.

21. And we poor humans are shown the city of God at Beersheba, where God the Father made an Eternal Covenant with us in Christ Jesus, as if within the repentant, shattered soul. When the poor soul entirely yields itself to this precious covenant and oath with a shattered heart of repentance, then the oath of God in the covenant of Jesus Christ stands open to it in Beersheba (that is, in the shattering of the soul); there God in Christ Jesus has sworn that he will not destroy the poor soul and its children and essence, nor inflict any harm upon this land of the soul, which is the body of humanity.

22. We should now place our trust in our dear **Emmanuel** <note>Hebrew: "God with us."</note> Jesus Christ, who swore a precious oath to his Father in our soulish property, that he will not turn his mercy and love away from us; we need only come to him in Beersheba and accept the oath as our own possession—that is, with a shattered, repentant heart.

For Phichol, the soul’s army commander—representing **Nature**—must rule and work in both evil and good during this life. He must be a heavy cross and constant temptation to the noble image of Christ (the new birth). That is, He gives birth to "heavenly twigs" within this repentant heart while it is still in the "foreign land" of the earthly man. He preaches from these new twigs concerning the name of the eternal God, and dwells for a long time—for the duration of the entire earthly life—within this Philistine hut.

## The 48th Chapter.

# How God tempted Abraham, and the figure of Christ’s sacrifice in His suffering and death presented.

->Genesis 22<-

After the Spirit in Moses had established and depicted the figure of the covenant of God in Christ Jesus with His children—showing how we poor children of Eve <note>original: "Hevæ Kinder."</note> should and must depart from this earthly will of selfhood <term>Selfhood: In Böhme's philosophy, "Eygenheit" refers to the egoistic, fallen will that acts for itself rather than for God.</term> and be born into a new will and life in Christ—He now presents the figure of how that would and should happen. He shows how Christ should offer our soul and humanity back to His Father; how He, as a sacrifice, should be cast into God's fire of wrath <term>Wrath-fire: Böhme's concept of the "Zorn-Feuer," the dark, consuming aspect of God's power that is transformed into Light through love and sacrifice.</term>; and how the human soul's selfhood and self-will should die in the fury of God, yet penetrate through death and the wrath of God with the single Divine Will. In doing so, He would shatter death—which held humanity captive—and put it to shame, thereby leading the human soul back to God His Father into the single, eternal Divine Will, and into the kingdom which He [prepared] for him in humanity...

->**...presented as Christ's sacrifice in His suffering and death.**<-

<margin>Chapter 48</margin>
1. ...had given to humanity—to surrender it back again, so that hereafter and in eternity God alone may be all in all, and the creature may no longer live by its own will, but rather resound only as an instrument of the Divine Voice in a Divine Harmony, and the entire Tree of Humanity may be only One in all its branches and limbs.

2. The Spirit in Moses clearly presents this figure until the end of all his writings, and plays with the inner figure <note>Böhme uses "figure" to mean a symbolic or prophetic archetype.</note>—which shall remain eternally—beneath the outer historical figure. Thus, I will also present this figure of Abraham’s temptation with his son Isaac in its spiritual form, explaining what is to be understood by it. For although the scholars have interpreted it to mean that God tempted Abraham to see if he would remain steadfast in faith, it has yet another, much deeper interpretation; for God already knows beforehand what man will do, and man cannot stand in temptation without His grace, as can be seen with Abraham when he denied his wife before King Abimelech when he moved to Gerar.

3. Here, Abraham is presented as Adam, and his son Isaac is presented as the humanity of Christ; and the voice that spoke to Abraham is the voice of God the Father. These three stand here as a figure of the process of the work of human redemption: how Abraham (that is, Adam) was to sacrifice his image in Isaac (that is, in Christ) to the Voice of God in the <term>Fire of God</term> <note>In Böhme’s thought, the "Fire" represents both God's rigorous justice and the transformative power that purifies the soul.</note>, so that humanity might be tested in the Fire of God.

4. So the Voice of God spoke to Abraham: "Abraham!" And he answered: "Here I am." That is: God called Adam in Abraham, as the representative of all people, and spoke: "Take Isaac, your only son, whom you love, and go into the land of Moriah, and offer him there as a burnt offering upon a mountain that I will tell you." Here, the Spirit looks with Isaac toward Christ: for in Isaac lay the Covenant and the <term>Faith-Ens</term> <note>original: "Glaubens-Ens." Böhme uses the Latin word "Ens" to describe an essential, spiritual substance or "being" that exists within the soul.</note> of Abraham, from which Christ was to come. So God's Voice spoke to Adam in Abraham: "Take your son whom you love and offer him as a burnt offering on the mountain that I will tell you." This means that the Jews, as Adam's children, were to offer Christ as a burnt sacrifice; that is, the Divine <term>Ens</term> was to give itself into the <term>Essence</term> <note>original: "Ente," likely a variation of "Entia" or "Ente" meaning essence/being.</note> of Adam, and Adam's children were to offer Him to God together in the Fire of God. It signifies that every person, once they have received the Faith-Ens, must sacrifice themselves entirely to God, and die to their own will in the Fire of God, and be born anew in the Divine Faith-Ens through the sacrifice in the Fire of God.

5. Thus the Spirit says in Moses: "Your son whom you love," meaning your own will, which has led itself into self-love. This self-will must be sacrificed to God, so that it may leave behind self-love in the Fire of God, and surrender its <term>Selfhood</term> <note>original: "Eigenheit." This refers to the state of being focused on one's own ego or "own-ness" rather than on God.</note> entirely, and no longer desire anything for itself...

...and live, but rather God [lives in me]; and it rightly indicates how Christ, in our human will—which in Adam had broken away or turned from God—was to sacrifice and surrender Himself entirely back to God His Father in Adam’s person. It shows how the <term>Wrath of God</term> <note>original: "Grimm Gottes," referring to the harsh, consuming aspect of the Divine nature</note> was to swallow up the will, specifically that will in which Adam had introduced himself into <term>Selfhood</term> <note>original: "Selbheit," the state of being centered on the ego rather than God</note>.

6. In this "swallowing up" by the <term>Fire of Wrath</term>, the <term>Love-Essence</term> <note>original: "Liebe-Ens"; Böhme uses the Latin "Ens" to mean the fundamental substance or being of Love</note>—found in the Word of Faith of Divine Power—should take hold of the true man created in Adam and preserve him within the consuming fire. This is just as **silver** and **gold** are tested on the <term>cupel</term> <note>original: "Teste," a shallow vessel used in refining precious metals</note>: while the copper and all other impurities vanish in smoke, only the gold or silver remains in the fire. In the same way, the assumed human "own-ness" <note>the tendency toward selfish possession</note>, along with the assumed serpent-like and animal-like essence—and everything that cannot subsist in the Divine Fire—was to be consumed in the sacrifice. This was done so that we, in the person of Christ, might again have a completely pure access and an open Wellspring of Grace. Thus was Christ to offer up our human will of "own-ness" to His Father, surrendering it back to Him. And specifically at Mount Moriah—that is, in His death and dying—He was to die to human Selfhood for everyone and in everything. It is just as when the trunk of a tree dies, all its branches die within it; yet as the tree rejuvenates itself, it also introduces its new power back into its branches. While this is certainly not possible in outward nature, it is quite possible in God—as seen in the **dry rod of Aaron**, which had died to its sap and life, yet in a single night turned green and bore beautiful almonds.

7. So God said, "upon a mountain that I will show you." This means it was not to happen according to Adam’s will; nor shall it happen in us according to our own will, as if we could prescribe for ourselves where and how we want to sacrifice ourselves to the Father in Christ, as **Babel** <note>Böhme's term for the confused, institutionalized, or "false" church</note> does. No; it must be upon the "mountain"—that is, in the place, in the quality, and in the death that the Lord sends to us. We must only be obedient like Abraham and surrender ourselves willingly into it when He wishes to sacrifice us to Himself. We are not to scourge, beat, or plague ourselves, but only to "sink down" <note>original: "ersincken," a mystical term for total passive surrender</note> with our will into Him, and wait until the Lord shows us the place where and how He will have us sacrificed. We should only offer Him our whole heart and will, with body and soul, and further entrust to Him what He will do with us. If He wishes to sacrifice us according to the body in the image of Jesus Christ, and when the Lord calls us to the sacrifice through His Cross, or wishes to offer us up to temporal death, then we should say with Abraham: *Here I am, Lord; do as You will.*

### Of Christ’s Sacrifice as Represented in His Suffering and Death

<margin>Chapter 48</margin>
...and took with him two young men and his son **Isaac**, and split wood for the burnt offering, and set out and went to the place of which God had told him.

->This figure is interpreted thus:<-

When the voice of God calls us, we should go immediately with **Abraham**. For "early" means when the voice breaks forth like a <term>Morning Glow</term> <note>original: "Morgenröthe," a central concept in Böhme’s theology representing the first dawning of divine light in the soul</note>, when God calls within us so that the thought strikes a person: "you should repent and turn back." This is the "early" hour. Then, he must immediately and with force "gird his donkey"—which represents the <term>animal man</term> <note>the physical, instinctual part of human nature</note>—even if that donkey cries out and says, "Wait, there is still time tomorrow." It must happen at the first sight of the will toward God. For this is the "hind that is hunted early," as the prophetic spirit signifies. <note>A reference to the title of Psalm 22, "The Hind of the Morning," which Christian tradition interprets as a prophecy of Christ's Passion.</note> For with the voice of God, **Christ** was to gird this donkey and go toward the sacrifice.

9. And the two young men whom **Abraham** took with him signify the <term>soul from the first principle</term> <note>original: "Principio," referring to the inward, spiritual source of the soul</note> and the <term>soul of this world</term>, which is the outward spirit of the external life. These must go with **Isaac** (that is, with **Christ**) in the "old **Abraham**" (who is **Adam**) toward God’s sacrifice. And **Abraham** (that is, the man **Adam** in his children) must himself "split the wood" upon which the sacrifice is to be burned. This means that when a person confesses **Christ**, he "splits the hearts of the godless" who hurry with him toward death and toward God's sacrifice. For **Adam** had split God's love and wrath within his humanity; now **Abraham** was to split the wood for the sacrifice. For **Christ** was also to split death and life apart from one another, and allow Himself to be sacrificed to God’s wrath upon that same split wood of death and life.

10. And on the third day, **Abraham** lifted up his eyes and saw the cities from afar. <note>The biblical text in Genesis 22:4 says he saw the "place" (Stätte); Böhme’s text or the transcription here says "cities" (Städte), likely interpreting the "place" as the New Jerusalem or the Kingdom of God.</note> Here the Spirit points to **Adam’s** sleep, when he fell asleep to the angelic world. On the third day after his falling asleep—now that the woman had been made from him and the Fall had occurred—he saw **Christ** from afar as the "Cities of God" within the Covenant. Also included in this is the Resurrection of **Christ** on the third day, when He saw His "cities" from afar—referring to when He would and should sacrifice and surrender mankind to God His Father. This represents the Last Judgment and the final sacrifice. It also signifies that **Abraham**, in the spirit, saw the sacrifice of **Christ** from afar as a future event, more than 2,000 years away. And when the Spirit says that **Abraham** lifted up his eyes on the third day and saw the cities, it means nothing else than that **Christ** lifted our human eyes up again toward God from the grave and from the dead on the third day, and that

# How God Tested Abraham, and the Figure

...even though it was still a long time off in Abraham's day, the Spirit thus plays with the <term>figure</term> <note>original: "Figur," meaning a prophetic type or symbolic representation of a future reality</note> toward that which is to come.

<margin>Gen. 22:5</margin>
11. And **Abraham** said to the two young men who went with him: "Stay here with the donkey; I and the lad will go yonder, and when we have worshipped, we will come back to you."

->This figure is understood inwardly thus.<-

The two young men with the donkey were to stay there and this time not go along to the sacrifice; only **Abraham** and **Isaac** were to perform that. This means that we, poor <term>children of Eve</term> <note>a traditional term for fallen humanity</note>, should—with our inner and outer souls, as with the <term>first and third Principle</term> <note>In Böhme’s system, the First Principle is the dark fire-source of the soul, and the Third is the physical, material world</note> of our life—remain for this time with the donkey (as with the outward body) here in this world. But **Christ** in **Isaac**, and **Abraham** in **Adam**, were to go to the sacrifice. That is: **Christ** stood in **Abraham’s** person as **Adam’s** representative, and also in his own **Heavenly Humanity**; he alone was to go and offer the sacrifice of his body to the <term>wrath-fire</term> of his Father, and worship/pray for us in God his Father. Therefore he said he would "go yonder"—that is, when he would offer up his life, he would go to God and pray for us before God.

12. This signifies his **Ascension** according to his humanity. When he had performed the sacrifice, he went "yonder" and prayed in our assumed humanity to God his Father. That is: our assumed soul, in Divine power and property, prays and intercedes for our weakness and ignorance in and before God. Therefore **Abraham** says: "We will go yonder and worship," which means **God** and **Man** together. And "when we have worshipped, we will come back to you"—that is, we poor children of **Eve** must meanwhile wait with the donkey until the time of his sacrifice and prayer is over; then he comes back to us, once we have completed the course of this outward, "donkey-like" life.

13. It also signifies that from the place where he has gone, when the time of his sacrifice in prayer is finished, he will certainly come back to us and dwell visibly among us in his created humanity. Just as the two angels said to the men of **Israel** when he ascended to heaven: "You shall see this **Jesus** come again, just as he has ascended." This time is now near, and his voice, preparing the **Bride**, has already resounded; and one should not consider this an uncertain fiction. The **Morning Star** and the **Messenger of the Annunciation** have appeared.

14. And **Abraham** took the wood and laid it upon **Isaac** his son, which was for the burnt offering; but he took the fire and the knife in his hand, and the two of them went together.

It distinguishes between the "animal" part of man that remains in the world and the "heavenly humanity" that enters into God's presence.</summary>

## The Inner Figure Stands Thus:

Adam had split God’s love and wrath within himself, and through his <term>creaturely life</term> <note>life focused on the self and created things rather than the Creator</note>, he led himself into the wrath, which had taken hold of earthly vanity. Now the Spirit of Moses points here to this same <term>figure</term> <note>a symbolic type or foreshadowing</note>: how Christ was to take our introduced sin upon himself and carry it to the fire-offering.

15. And **Abraham** took the knife and fire: **Abraham** signifies **Adam**, who took the <term>wrath-fire</term> <note>the harsh, judging aspect of God's nature in Böhme’s theology</note> of God into himself; and the knife signifies death—indicating that **Christ** was to be killed and sacrificed to the Father within **Abraham’s** (that is, **Adam’s**) wrath-fire. It clearly indicates that **Abraham** (that is, **Adam**) was to do this to **Christ**, for **Christ** was to be sacrificed by men. Because the man **Adam** had taken upon himself the fire-wood (representing sin) for the sacrifice, so too must man (acting through the Jews) sacrifice to the wrath of God, so that man might be reconciled through man—meaning through the humanity of **Christ**.

16. Then **Isaac** spoke to his father **Abraham**: "My father." **Abraham** answered: "Here I am, my son." And he said: "See, here is fire and wood, but where is the sheep for the burnt offering?" **Abraham** answered: "My son, God will provide for himself a sheep for the burnt offering." And the two of them went on together.

## The Precious Figure Stands Thus.

The Spirit here plays in the person of **Christ**, who had come in great humility into **Adam’s** humanity, and presents himself to his Father in **Adam’s** essence with his own **Heavenly Humanity**, saying: "See, my Father, here I have taken sin and death in humanity upon myself; here now is the fire of your wrath—the divided forms of life characterized by human property, self-interest, and self-will. In this I now have the wood, in which your wrath-fire burns. Here I have the wood (the sin of all people) and also your fire for the sacrifice; where now is the sheep—the patient **Lamb**—that is to be sacrificed in this fire?" And **Abraham** answered out of his strong <term>faith-essence</term> <note>original: "Glaubens-Ente," referring to the spiritual substance or inner being of faith</note>: "My son, God will provide for himself a sheep for the burnt offering," and the two of them went on together.

17. Here **Christ** presents himself to his Father in the figure of **Isaac** within our assumed humanity, and says: "Where now is the sheep for the true sacrifice of reconciliation?" But **Abraham’s** faith had grasped the patient sheep which lay within **Isaac**—that is, the **Heavenly Humanity** which God wanted to reveal in the faith-essence within our faded, formerly heavenly humanity...

# How God Tested Abraham / and the Symbolism

<margin><image-desc>A small hand-drawn symbol or monogram near the top left of the text block.</image-desc></margin>
...and said, "God will provide for himself a sheep for the right burnt offering": and he points secretly to the **Heavenly Humanity**, which God would introduce into **Christ’s humanity**, as if into our own humanity. That was to be the patient **sheep** which God would provide for himself, which **Abraham** had already grasped through faith and pointed toward.

<margin><image-desc>A decorative bracket with three points and arrow-like flourishes pointing towards the start of paragraph 18.</image-desc></margin>
18. And when the Spirit of **Moses** says, "And the two of them went on together," referring to the sacrifice, this indicates our **Adamic humanity** and **Christ’s Heavenly, supernatural humanity** of Divine essence. It shows that these two should go together to the sacrifice of God, just as **Christ** then sacrificed his Heavenly humanity within our humanity to the Father on the Cross. With the Heavenly nature, he reconciled our nature—which was imprisoned in the <term>wrath of God</term> <note>In Böhme’s thought, the 'wrath' is the harsh, consuming fire of God's power when separated from His love</note>—and preserved it in the fire of God's wrath, just as gold is preserved in the fire by the <term>tincture</term> <note>An alchemical term used here to describe a spiritual substance that transforms and perfects base matter</note>.

19. And when they came to the place which God had told him, **Abraham** built an altar there and laid the wood upon it, and bound his son **Isaac**. He laid him on the altar on top of the wood and stretched out his hand and took the knife to slaughter his son. This is now the "earnestness" or the <term>figure</term> <note>A symbolic type or prophetic foreshadowing</note> of how God intended to bind his Son through **Adam’s** children (that is, through **Abraham’s** children, the Jews), which means to bind our sin and lay it upon the wood. This signifies hanging him on the Cross, as a figure of the **Holy Trinity**. This Trinity was once within man, but it had become a wooden, earthly cross; whereas previously, the **Life-Cross** (as the figure of the Deity) had been spiritual and holy in **Adam**, it had made itself earthly and "wooden" through earthly lust. Therefore, death—as the dying of the holy Cross within man—must be sacrificed back to God on a wooden, earthly cross, and be transformed once again out of earthly death into the holy-spiritual figure.

20. **Christ** was not to be slaughtered, but hung up and pierced in his hands and feet. For the wrath of God had been awakened by the conduct of the "work of our hands" and the "walking of our feet." Therefore, **Isaac**, acting as the figure of **Christ**, also must not be slaughtered and also not burned; for he was not the "right" one, but only the figure within our humanity. He could not fulfill this sacrifice through his own strengths. This indicates that we may well be bound and laid upon the wood with **Christ**, and must even die for **Christ’s** sake; but we cannot achieve this sacrifice through our own death so that we might complete it ourselves in God’s wrath-fire and reconcile God through our death. **Christ** alone has done it. Just as **Isaac** could not do it, but the <term>Faith-Ens</term> <note>original: "Glaubens-Ens"; refers to the spiritual "being" or "substance" of faith</note> within **Abraham** and **Isaac**, from which **Christ** arose, performed it—and can still do it today in Christians, through **Christ** in his humanity within us.

->Represented by Christ’s Sacrifice in his Suffering and Death.<-

<margin>Chapter 48.</margin>
21. And just as Isaac was presented as a <term>type of Christ</term> <note>original: "Christi Figur"; a 'type' is an Old Testament person or event that foreshadows something in the life of Christ</note>, as if he were to be the sacrifice: so too must every true Christian enter into that same pattern with Isaac. They must willingly surrender themselves into the death of Christ, binding their sins through their will in the Spirit of Christ and offering them upon the Altar of Christ, being ready to die to sin. Then the voice of God comes—just as it happened to Abraham, and to Hagar in the wilderness of Beersheba—and says: "Do nothing to your nature, which is your son: for now I know that you believe in God."

22. However, the repentant sinner must reach the same point as Abraham and Isaac did here; Isaac was already bound upon the wood, and Abraham had grasped the knife to slaughter him. It must be such an earnest matter that the sinful human binds their sin with all their senses and mind, surrendering themselves entirely to the <term>Process</term> <note>In Böhme’s theology, the 'Process' is the lived experience of spiritual transformation and the imitation of Christ’s life</note>, willing now to die to sin and to offer it into Christ’s death through faith and trust in God. Like Abraham, the person must take the knife in hand—that is, they must fully resolve in their mind to perform the work of earnest repentance and die to sin. It must come to the actual doing of it, and not merely standing before the altar saying: "I am a sinner; God has sacrificed Christ for me," while still holding onto the sinful will. Instead, one must bind sin into Christ’s death and, with all one's strength, lay oneself upon the wood of this <term>burnt offering altar</term>.

23. The evil earthly will must be bound and surrendered in earnest, cast upon God’s altar into Christ’s death, and sacrificed along with Christ's dying. It is not enough to merely comfort the "rogue" <note>original: "Schalck"; referring to the clever, deceptive, and unrepentant part of the human ego</note> and "tickle" it with Christ’s death, saying that God accepts Christ’s payment on our behalf and that we need only comfort ourselves and accept it from the outside. No, no: that will not do. Rather, one must die to sin within Christ's death, "put on" <note>an allusion to Galatians 3:27, "putting on Christ" like a garment</note> Christ's sacrifice in his death, and—as an obedient Isaac—rise again within Christ and with him through God’s mercy in the Spirit and Will of Christ. In this way, God justifies us from the altar of the sin-offering, just as he did with Isaac in Christ, who is the true sacrifice prefigured by Isaac.

24. It is not as <term>Babel</term> <note>Böhme’s derogatory name for the institutional, "confused" churches of his day, which he believed taught a superficial faith</note> teaches; it must be a matter of earnestness and not merely "comfort." We must obey God as Abraham did; only then do we "put on" Christ’s suffering and death. Only then does Christ’s death count within us, and only then can it be said: "You have been saved by grace through Christ's merit." The will of <term>selfhood</term> <note>original: "Selbheit"; the self-centered ego that seeks its own way apart from God</note> does not achieve this; only the one who enters into Christ's death and dies achieves it. It must come to the death of the "own-will," so that the soul’s will becomes disgusted by the sin in the flesh (the lusts of the flesh), and they become enemies. Otherwise, Christ’s death is of no use to anyone.

->## On the Death of Sarah and the Hereditary Burial Place of Abraham / what is indicated and to be understood therein. Genesis 23.<-

The Spirit in Moses has presented the entire **figure** <term>original: "Figur"; in this context, a symbolic representation or spiritual blueprint</term> of man through Abraham: what his condition in this world shall be, and what becomes of him afterward. For as he first spoke of the beginning—as if speaking of the trunk of the human tree from whence it sprouted—he afterward indicates its boughs and branches, alongside its strength and virtue. He reports how this tree, in its strength and **essence**, was corrupted, and how God applied the highest **tincture** <term>original: "Tinctur"; an alchemical term used by Böhme to describe a spiritual "medicine" or transformative force</term> upon it to "tinge" <note>to dye or imbue with spiritual quality</note> and renew it once more; and how the poison in the essence of this tree was resisted.

2. Here he now indicates in a quite wondrous way how this tree, in its corrupted property, stood in a "foreign field" and rooted itself with its root into a foreign characteristic, in which the root was not at home; and how the root of the "human-tree" must leave the foreign field along with the foreign, introduced essence, and give itself up quite freely out of its life-will and desire.

3. It is also indicated thereby how the place from which the human root sprouted was between the holy spiritual world and this corrupted world. As man’s "property" <note>referring to man's essential nature or inheritance</note> originated from there, it stands in a "double cave"—as if in two **principles** <term>Böhme's term for the fundamental realms of existence: Light/Heaven and Darkness/Fire</term>. He must be buried again into this same double cave, just as a grain of seed is sown into a field; and how this same double cave is man's rightful property, of whose being he himself is essentially composed.

4. We see the **figure** of this here with Abraham: while he wandered in this outer world, he was to possess no land of his own on earth, but moved from one place to another and was a stranger everywhere. But when his Sarah died, he desired a hereditary burial place for his wife, and also for himself and his children. Furthermore, he did not want it for free, but wished to buy it. All of this is a quite wondrous formation and not merely a bare history, as the Jews have held it to be, while the "veil of Moses" <note>original: "Deckel Moyſis"; a reference to the biblical idea that the spiritual meaning of scripture is hidden from those who read it only literally</note> hung before their eyes. We, however, wish to place the inner figure alongside the outer one and see what the Spirit in Moses indicates here.

5. Moses says: Sarah died at Hebron, in the capital city in the land of Canaan. The history may indeed be so, but the Spirit has its **figure** beneath it, for it looks toward the **Center** <term>original: "Centrum"; the spiritual heart or point of origin</term> where the death of the saints is.

### ...to take a wife for his son Isaac, etc.

<margin>Chapter 24.</margin>

12. If a person is unwilling, the same Word falls upon another who is capable of receiving it. Therefore, Nature—acting as the **messenger** <note>original: "Bott"</note> or **steward** <note>original: "Amptmann"; an official who manages an estate</note> or promoter of the heavenly message—must not lead the Word, along with the Divine **Essence** <term>Ens: a term used by Böhme to describe the fundamental spiritual "substance" or "being" of a thing</term>, back to that original place (that is, into the inner Divine Voice). For whatever God once speaks forth into power through His Word must stand in a Divine form for Divine contemplation. Nature should proceed on its way like a messenger, proclaiming that the Father has given all His goods to Isaac. This means He has given all His goods to Christ, and now He demands a wife—representing the human being—who enters into a state of marriage with Isaac in Christ.

13. Then the servant laid his hand under the hip of his master Abraham and swore this to him. This signifies when God sank His holy Word—with its heavenly **essence** <term>Ens</term> or being, as the "shaped Wisdom"—into the natural **essence of Mary** <note>original: "Ens Mariæ"</note>, as if into God’s servant, and transformed God and man into one person. In this way, human nature swore an oath under the "hip" of the Father’s Eternal Nature in God: that it would be obedient to God, go forth from that moment on, seek the human "wife," and take her into marriage for the Divine **essence** <term>Ens</term>. All of this is to be understood as occurring in the person of Christ. In His assumed humanity, acting as the servant of Abraham (or God His Father) in His natural capacity, Christ was to go out with His Word and seek this woman as His bride, whom the angel of the Lord (as the Divine Will) should **bring to him** <gloss>lead to</gloss>.

14. So the servant took ten camels from his master’s camels and departed, carrying with him all kinds of his master’s goods; he set out and went toward Mesopotamia to the city of Nahor. Here the Spirit perceives the **process of God** <note>original: "Proceß Gottes"; the systematic unfolding of God's plan in the material world</note>: how God sent His angel or messenger Gabriel, using the voice of nature, to the human nature at Nahor—that is, to Adam’s nature within the **essence of Mary** <term>Ens Mariæ</term>. In this voice, the living holy Word was hidden within the heavenly living **essence** <term>Ens</term>. The Father’s nature sent along "ten camels"—these are the ten forms of the three **Principles** <term>Principien: Böhme’s framework of the three "worlds" or dimensions (the Dark World, the Light World, and the Outward World)</term> for both the natural and supernatural "fire-life." These consist of the seven forms of the **Center of Nature** <note>original: "Centri der Natur"; the foundational forces that cause life to manifest</note> and the three forms of the three distinctions of the Principles. All of these together are "God’s camels," by which He carries and supports all things.

15. And the "master’s goods" are the "shaped Wisdom" of the great wonders and powers. God’s **steward** <note>original: "Amptmann"</note> took all this with him when he carried the Divine Word within himself and introduced or revealed it into the human natural **essence** <term>Ens</term> (into the **essence of Mary** <term>Ens Mariæ</term>). This describes how one might attempt to speak of the great deeds of God, even though the external, dense, sensory tongue cannot provide enough words to satisfy deep **spiritual understanding** <note>original: "Mentalischen verstande"; a conceptual or intuitive grasp that transcends literal language</note>.

30. He does not send them to the "snake-beasts," for they do not hear God’s word; they have no capacity for it, just as the Canaanites in their snake-essence <note>original: "Ente"</note> were entirely animalistic and half-dead to divine hearing because of their malice and self-will.

32. And the noble Virgin speaks to the will of God: "Drink, my lord; I will also draw for your camels." Understand by the "camels" the essences of human nature derived from the Father's property; and by the "Virgin" understand the nature and property of the Light in Love, the essence of the Divine Being <note>original: "Entis"</note> of the Angelic World. This is what faded in Adam, and through this drawing of water, it returns to its bridegroom, the soul.

He also runs to the well of the Word of God and begs God to enter into him with His Word, just as Laban here begged Abraham’s servant to enter his home. # ...to take a wife for his son Isaac, etc.

<margin>Chapter 50</margin>
39. Thus also does human nature act: when it hears Christ sounding within the inner man, and sees the jewelry which the Holy Spirit has hung upon the **Virginly Image**, then Laban—acting as the brother of the inner image—asks the will of God to come and dwell within him.

40. And when the will of God (represented by Abraham’s servant) has moved into Bethuel and Laban (representing the <term>Third Principle <note>In Böhme’s philosophy, the "Third Principle" is the visible, material world and the external human life, as opposed to the spiritual realms of light or darkness.</note></term> of humanity), then **God’s Steward** <note>original: "Amptmann Gottes," referring here to the Word of God that acts as an agent in the soul.</note>—which is the Word of God entering the human being—speaks: "I will not eat of your food (meaning the essence of the external life) until I first deliver my message: that you give your sister, the **Heavenly Virginity**, as a wife to my Lord—meaning the son of my Lord, the humanity of Jesus Christ." And he recounts to human nature how God has orchestrated this; that is, he opens the **Divine Understanding**, so that the natural man learns to understand God’s will, to which he was previously blind.

41. At that point, poor nature, along with the soul, surrenders to the will of God. Then Laban and Bethuel speak: "This comes from the Lord; we should not speak against it. Behold, here is your place; do with me and my inner self as you will. Here is Rebecca, the **formed Word of heavenly quality**; take her and marry her to your Lord’s son—the humanity of JESUS CHRIST—according to your pleasure, as the Lord has spoken."

42. One sees quite clearly here how the Spirit of Moses speaks in figures; for he places Laban, as Bethuel's son, before the father. He places the outer soul before the inner **Fire-soul**, and the **Air-soul** before the true **Fire-soul**; though they are not two souls, but one, understood in two <term>principles <note>original: "Principiis." Böhme views the soul as a singular entity that functions across different spiritual dimensions or "principles."</note></term>. For the fire-soul gives its answer through the air-soul. The fire-soul possesses the "uncompacted" <note>meaning unarticulated or raw power</note> tongue, but the air-soul possesses the "compacted," formed speech.

43. Therefore, the Spirit of Moses puts Laban, Rebecca’s brother, at the forefront, as if the business were carried out by Laban. This is to indicate that when **God’s Steward** (the will of God drawing the person toward the Father) enters into the human being and petitions for a lodging and for the Virgin, the **outer spirit** of the human must give the consent. For the outer spirit has been turned away from God and true yieldedness; now it must entirely surrender its will back into the will of God.

44. And when this happens—when the outer soul and the inner fire-soul fully consent to this marriage and surrender themselves to God—then the will of God, as the Steward in the drawing of the Father, bows down...

49. 50. Oh, what a heartfelt meal is held there! Where this wedding is held within a person—which no Canaanite serpent-man <note>A term used by Böhme to describe a person ruled by their fallen, earthly, or "serpentine" nature, who is closed off to spiritual truth.</note> is worthy to know or to taste. ->This stands in the Inner Figure <note>The "Inner Figure" refers to the hidden spiritual or mystical meaning of the biblical story.</note> thus.<-

51. But this wedding does not last forever; rather, as soon as Abraham's servant had obtained the virgin and held the meal and wedding with the father, mother, and Laban, and had remained there overnight, he stood up early and said: "Let me depart to my master."

52. When Christ has married Himself to the Virgin Sophia, as the inner humanity, the voice of God sounds shortly thereafter in the soul and says: "I will depart from you with the Virgin." It is always as if He wants to break camp and depart from the person, so that the poor soul must forever beg and plead that He might stay with her a little longer. But the voice often sounds: "Do not hold me back; I must depart or travel to my Lord; you are evil and sinful; I may no longer remain with you."

53. Thus, one day is drawn out after another, and yet Christ departs with His bride into His fatherland—that is, into the second Principle <note>In Böhme’s cosmology, the "Second Principle" is the world of light and divine love (Heaven), as opposed to the "First Principle" (dark fire-world) and the "Third Principle" (the visible material world).</note>—though the wedding is held in all three Principles.

How Abraham took another wife, etc.

<margin>Chapter 51.</margin>

# The 51st Chapter.

## How Abraham took another wife, with whom he fathered six more sons, to whom he gave gifts, and gave all his goods to his son Isaac, but let the others depart from him during his lifetime; and how he died, and what is to be understood by this.
->Genesis 25<-

Moses says: Abraham took another wife named Keturah, who bore him Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah, from whom six lineages arose. With Sarah, Abraham fathered only one son, whom the entire history concerns; but with Keturah he fathered six sons, of whom nothing special is reported except for their lineage.

->This is understood inwardly as follows.<-

Abraham and his Sarah had to become very old before he fathered Isaac: indicating that Christ should be revealed in the flesh in the old age of the world.

2. Isaac was fathered out of Abraham's nature and out of the <term>essence of faith</term> <note>original: "Glaubens-Ente." In Böhme's mystical vocabulary, this refers to the spiritual substance or "being" that is formed through faith.</note>, conceived in an old, almost dead <term>matrix</term> <note>original: "Matrice." Referring to the womb or generative source, which in Sarah's old age was naturally barren.</note> according to human nature, so that God’s <term>Ens</term> <note>original: "Ens." A Latin term for "being" or "essence." Böhme uses it to describe the divine spiritual seed or substance that takes precedence over natural matter.</note> might have the precedence. But when Sarah died, Abraham took Keturah, and soon fathered six sons with her: Keturah expresses in her name the <term>center of nature</term>; when one forms the sensory, uncompacted spirits of the letters into this word "Keturah," one understands that Keturah is a formed matrix of nature. This indicates that after Abraham had fathered the prototype of Christ in the essence of faith, he should now father his own likeness according to <term>Adam’s nature</term> <note>The fallen, earthly nature of humanity inherited from the first man.</note> out of the six qualities of the natural spirit-life, and represent his own natural image as well; therefore he also had to have such a vessel for that purpose.

3. Sarah was to bear only one son: to indicate that the kingdom of men is given only to one, and that they all belong under this one, and in him should become that same one, like branches on a tree, which Christ should be in everyone.

4. But here Abraham now fathered six sons with Keturah, according to the six qualities of formed nature and the operation of the six <term>days of creation</term> <note>original: "Tagwercke," literally "day-works." Böhme correlates the six sons with the six days of work in Genesis, representing the temporal, natural world.</note>;

...and Isaac—that is, Christ—is the seventh, serving as the day of rest or Sabbath, into which the six sons were to enter into rest, just like the six days of creation. Understand this as the six properties of the <term>center of nature</term> <note>original: "Centri der Natur." In Böhme's philosophy, these are the fundamental forces that constitute existence before they find balance in the "seventh" property, which is divine rest or harmony.</note>—the active spirit-life—resting in the seventh. Thus also the Spirit of God represented this figure in Abraham.

5. And here we have a very beautiful symbolic figure against those who are "wise in their own reason," who say: "Whoever is not born by nature in the <term>essence of faith</term> <note>original: "Glaubens-Ente." Böhme uses the word "Ente" (Ens) to mean a spiritual substance or seed.</note> is hardened in heart and cannot come to the state of being God's child; he is not drawn by God so that he may come to the new birth." This symbolic figure strikes their trifles to the ground and points to the true foundation. First, it presents Isaac as Christ, showing that the Kingdom of God belongs to Him alone by right of inheritance, and that no human being can possess it by natural right anymore. It shows how we, along with Adam, were all cast out from it and lost it, just as Keturah’s children were all excluded from Abraham’s goods, which Isaac alone inherited.

6. Beside this, it shows how Adam’s children were also born from Abraham, and how he gave them gifts from his possessions. This signifies how gifts are given to Adam’s natural children from the riches of God the Father and Christ—how Abraham’s goods are given to them by grace as a gift.

7. For Abraham did not cast out his natural children without a gift. In the same way, God did not cast Adam out of Paradise without his gift: He gave him, from that moment on, the <term>Serpent-Treader</term> <note>original: "Schlangentreter." A reference to the promise in Genesis 3:15 that the offspring of the woman would crush the head of the serpent; here it refers to Christ.</note> in the Word of the Covenant. Afterward, He cast Adam out of the childhood inheritance of natural right, but accepted him again through that gift. Just as here Abraham did not reject his children from their status as children—for they were dear to him—but only from the natural right to his goods. Therefore, he gave them gifts from his possessions. By this, he signifies that although the Kingdom of Heaven belongs only to Christ as the true Isaac, just as God gave the Covenant to Adam by grace, and just as Abraham gave gifts to the children of the concubines <note>original: "Kebsweiber."</note> out of Isaac’s right, so today God the Father still gives the Covenant and the inheritance of Christ as a gift to the natural children of Adam and Abraham.

8. And just as Abraham’s natural children were not disinherited from the Covenant, but only from his worldly goods, so also is no human being disinherited from the Covenant of God established in Adam and Abraham. Everyone receives the gifted Covenant while still in the mother's womb, wherein they have the power, within their gifted Covenant, to turn toward the riches of Christ.

<summary>Böhme argues that while the Kingdom of Heaven belongs to Christ (Isaac) by right, all humanity (the children of the concubines) receives a share of divine grace as a "gift" through the Covenant. He uses this to refute the idea that some people are naturally excluded from salvation, asserting that the "gift" is present in everyone from the womb.</summary>
