In Böhme’s theology, the "Pearl" or "Pearl-spirit" represents the precious spark of divine wisdom and the Sophia (heavenly wisdom) hidden within the soul.</note> is not known / the wise nevertheless look into the eyes of that spirit and recognize him / seeing that God has given him His wisdom and spirit / and they take his writings and teachings / and direct their whole lives accordingly; thus Joseph sits in the office of regent for Pharaoh’s steward / and governs his entire house.

56. But with this, Joseph has not yet passed through the judgment / for in this position of governance, he first faces the greatest danger of his life. For it is there that the steward’s wife first burned with lust toward him / representing the **false sects** / which wish to mingle with his spirit / and altogether deck themselves out with it for the sake of temporal honor and art. And when this spirit of Joseph will not mix with their human **trumpery** <note>original: "Tandt," meaning trifles or worthless finery.</note> / then they first cry out, "Alas!" and "Woe!" over him and accuse him of unchastity / as if it were false doctrine / and they denounce him before the steward / that is / before the worldly authorities.

57. There Joseph must first sit in the dungeon and in prison / and be properly tested / until God draws him out and places him before King Pharaoh; only then does his wisdom and fear of God become manifest / so that it is recognized / that his understanding is given to him by God / and thus his understanding is set as a regent over the land of Egypt / who governs not only foreign peoples / but his brothers also must finally come to him in their **famine** <note>original: "Thewrung." This refers both to the physical famine in Genesis and a spiritual "dearth" or scarcity of divine knowledge.</note> / when the right understanding of divine knowledge becomes scarce among them / and he also nourishes them with his wisdom. And thus God led him ahead of their father / so that they must afterward come / and seek and enjoy their brother Joseph’s wisdom among foreign peoples.

58. For in this way, Israel also persecuted the prophets / until they fell into darkness and idolatry in the lusts of their flesh / and everything that the prophets had told them came upon them. Then, when they sat in hunger and misery and their land was full of abominations / they sought out the writings of the prophets and only then recognized / that their speech was true / and that they had done them wrong; and they decorated their graves and said: "Had we lived in our fathers' time / we would not have wanted to kill them." But the Most High holds His judgment in such a way / that He [judges] the house...

59. Joseph was sold for 20 pieces of silver and Christ for 30. A term from alchemy used by Böhme to describe the spiritual essence or "inner quality" that gives life and character to a being.</note> He sprouted from the property of the Light; whereas the Adamic soul is of the Fire, from which the Light takes its origin and revelation. Thus, in Christ, the property of the Light took the property of the Fire (the Adamic soul) into itself, and the inner hidden essence turned itself outward again—which in Adam had been sealed up and had faded from the life of the Light.

60. Therefore, because a Christian is under Christ, and in Christ becomes revealed again in God, the figure of Christ stands in the number 30, and that of a Christian in the number 20 as presented in this figure; for a Christian is sold into human hands to suffer. But Christ had to suffer not only in human hands, but also surrender Himself to the wrath of God, from which He sweated blood.

61. And this whole figure is powerfully prefigured <note>original: "præfiguriret."</note> in Joseph, showing how a Christian stands in his figure before God and the world; for the entire history of Joseph demonstrates how Adam becomes a Christian, how he must be placed into the <term>Process</term> <note>original: "Proceß." This refers to the specific path of spiritual suffering, death of the old self, and rebirth that mirrors Christ’s life.</note> of Christ, in Christ’s figure, and become an image of Christ; and how God exalts him again in Christ’s <term>Process</term> in the kingdom of Christ and sets him at the right hand of God, just as Joseph was set at the right hand of King Pharaoh after he had stood in Christ’s <term>Process</term> and been led through it.

# Chapter 65.

## Concerning Judah and Tamar: A hidden figure of Adam and Christ: in which the new Rebirth is excellently prefigured.

### On the 38th Chapter of Genesis.

When one considers the history of Joseph according to outward reason, reason says: Why does Joseph’s history not stand sequentially in the Bible, since it occurred sequentially? Why does Moses place this figure of Judah and Tamar in between? But if we look at and contemplate this history of Judah and Tamar, and then Joseph’s figure with right understanding, we see that the Holy Spirit has placed them in this order with great diligence and quite correctly.

### Of Judah and Tamar

27. The prophetic spirit of Grace cried out: "Dear, let me come to you, lie with me; I will give you the seed of my nature." Yet Judah did not recognize that God was within his spirit, and he desired to mingle with it in a creaturely <note>referring to the physical, earthly world of created things</note> way. He also did not recognize that this prophetic spirit was the embodied angel of the Covenant within man himself: so utterly blind was the Adamic nature <term>Adamische Natur</term><note>the fallen state of humanity after the exile from Eden</note> toward the Covenant.

28. The Adamic nature thought it was a whore, for she presented herself as such in the prophetic spirit; for this reason, the Jews very often killed the prophets: because they believed they heard a false, whoring spirit speaking. And here, with Judah, was the figure <note>a "figure" or "type" is a historical event that prefigures a spiritual truth</note> of how the first Adamic nature should mingle with the Covenant of Grace, how the Heavenly Essence <term>Ens</term><note>from the Latin for "being"; Böhme uses it to mean a spiritual or divine substance</note> would take the Adamic-human nature back into itself, and how man himself would not understand what God was doing with him.

29. The Adamic nature would indeed yearn in its lust for the Heavenly Essence <term>Ens</term>, but it would not know it; even if it were to see it, it would think, "This is my equal; I will play the whore with it," for Paradise has become foreign to Adam.

30. And as Tamar stood on the way for Judah with her face covered, and he spoke to her: "Sleep with me"; then Tamar spoke to Judah: "What will you give me, that you may lie with me?" He spoke: "I will send you a young goat from the herd." She answered: "Then give me a pledge until you send it to me." He spoke: "What pledge do you want me to give you?" And she answered: "Your ring, and your cord, and your staff which you have in your hands." Then he gave them to her and lay with her, and she became pregnant by him. And she rose and went away, and laid aside the cloak, and put on her widow's clothes again.

31. Here the Spirit plays quite beautifully in the figure <note>the symbolic representation</note>, showing how Adam's nature philanders <note>original: "buhlet," meaning to court or woo, often with illicit connotations</note> with the presented "new Eve" in the Covenant, yet does not know her; and how the Covenant philanders with Adam’s first true nature—how two foreign forms come together. When Adam's nature says, "Sleep with me," it wishes to have this Eve of the Covenant only for a brief moment of pleasure. The Adamic nature acts in its selfhood in such a way that it only woos the new Eve with a false appearance, and its heart is far from the true, holy marriage; it approaches her only with a hypocritical whoredom, as happens in the office of the Pharisees <note>referring to religious leaders who value outward ritual over inward transformation</note>. Thus, this Eve speaks to the Adamic nature: "What will you give me?" Then the Adamic nature promises a goat; that is, an animalistic will full of the heat of hypocrisy.

It indicates to us here that the Adamical harlotry and abominations are laid bare before this **Covenant of Grace**; and that man, in such abominations, is guilty of the hellish fire—just as Judah judged his daughter-in-law Tamar to the condemnation of fire, not recognizing that he himself was the "harlot-man" who stood in equal condemnation.

52. Here the Spirit also represents in this **figure** the false judgments of men: that they do the very same things they judge. Just as Judah here condemned Tamar's harlotry to the fire, yet did not see his own fall—that he himself was the guilty party. This signifies that Christ would also place Himself within the world's judgment in this **Line of the Covenant** <note>original: "Bundes Linea" — the genealogical and spiritual lineage leading to the Messiah.</note> as a righteous judge, who wished to separate the unrighteous from the righteous and condemn the world's harlotry and idolatry. But conversely, we see in this **figure** how Tamar presented the pledge—the ring, cord, and staff—before the judgment and before the heavy sentence of Judah. With these, she set aside Judah's passed sentence and stilled his wrath, so that he had to have mercy on her and grant her justice.

53. Thus also did this **figure** stand before God in the inner ground with Judah and Tamar, and with Adam and Eve. For Adam had led himself into fleshy, earthly lust, and had "harloted" with his own feminine quality <note>A reference to the Boehmian concept of the "Sophia" or the heavenly feminine principle from which Adam fell.</note> through **imagination** <term>Imagination: In this context, it refers to the creative or "imaging" power of the mind that can either lead toward God or toward earthly, beastly desires.</term> in a beastly manner, and [lost] the heavenly, magical way...

### Of Judah and Tamar

<margin>Judah</margin>...forgot every Divine marriage; therefore his heavenly wife also <note>original: "st" — likely *stund* (stood) or *starb* (died), meaning the spiritual nature ceased to function.</note> and in her place the earthly animalistic nature awoke, with which he practiced fornication in a beastly manner. God placed this in him, as in <margin>Eve</margin> Adam himself, into His judgment and wanted to condemn Adam to death, as he was condemned by God's justice.

54. But the re-embodied Eve in the **Covenant of Grace**, who was embodied in the first Eve—as in the seed of the faded woman <note>A reference to the "seed of the woman" from Genesis 3:15, which the author sees as a spiritual essence preserved from the heavenly world.</note> from the essence of the heavenly world—stepped before God's strict judgment and spoke to God's justice: "Behold, I am pregnant by the man to whom these belong"; that is: "Behold, I have taken Adam's soul, spirit, and body as a pledge, when I mixed with him again and was married to him. I have taken the Father's nature, which was in awakened wrath, into my love; and I am now pregnant with human nature and shall give birth to a **God-Man**."

55. And when the Father's property <term>Property: In this mystical context, an "attribute" or "essential quality" of God's nature.</term> in the soulful nature of man recognized that the Father had himself sown her again into grace—as into the new Eve in the Covenant—the wrath of the Father in the soul spoke (as this grace stepped toward him) to this new Eve: "You are more righteous than I, for I caused the impurity of Adam, so that he became earthly and committed harlotry before me." And I did not give Shelah <note>Judah’s third son, whom he withheld from Tamar.</note> to the new Eve as a husband; that is, I did not give the Word for the new **Rebirth** <term>Wiedergeburt: The spiritual process of being born again into a divine state.</term> through the Law and in the Law. Therefore, Tamar—as the new Eve during the time of the Law—dallied with Judah and his children in the soulful and human nature, and left Shelah (as a figure of the Law) standing aside. The grace of the new Eve in the Covenant has always mixed with God's children, as can be seen in the Saints, especially the Prophets, who outwardly lived under and practiced the Law, and yet always mixed with the new Eve of grace, living not according to the Law, but to grace.

56. And this is the powerful **figure** in this place: how the Covenant of the Promise in Judah and the awakening of the Covenant in the "Woman’s Seed" have always stood against each other, and dallied with each other in love toward the future manifestation in the flesh of Christ.

57. For this figure of Judah and Tamar is, in its inner ground, nothing other than this very thing. Externally, the whorish, evil Adam with his fleshly Eve is placed in the figure as the external "man of sins" in a sinful form; but internally, it is the marriage of the new union in the **Rebirth**.

Namely, when Christ is revealed in a person, 
<margin>draws</margin>
He points out <note>original: "zeiget... an."</note> to that person the 30 pieces of silver for which He was sold unto suffering and death. He draws this suffering and death toward the person, in whom the typology of the 30 pieces of silver—representing how He was betrayed and 
<margin>sets</margin>
sold—stands grafted. In this way, the person is grafted, planted, or etched into the suffering and death of Christ. Thus, the person becomes a Christian in Christ's suffering and death, and stands in the form of Christ, losing the right to his own natural will as well as the kingdom of this world.

5. For in Christ’s death, he dies to this world according to his inner spiritual person, and according to that same inner person, he is no longer in the world but in Christ, in God, as in the Kingdom of God, even as it is written: *The Kingdom of God is within you.* <note>Luke 17:21</note> Likewise: *Examine yourselves to see if Christ has taken shape in you.* <note>Galatians 4:19</note> Likewise: *You are temples of the Holy Spirit who dwells in you.* Likewise: *You are Christ's servants, and you shall eat the flesh of the Son of Man; thus He remains in you and you in Him, and without Him you have no life.* Just as a herb or grass, as well as all earthly things, has no life, growth, or effect within itself without the power of the sun, so too the person, without the Divine Sun—which has revealed itself through Christ in His Christians—has no life or salvation outside of Christ within themselves.

6. And just as Christ was sold for 30 pieces of silver unto suffering and death—which 30 pieces of silver signify the 30 years of Christ before His baptism, before He entered into His office and Divine governance according to His humanity, wherein He surrendered His human will to God and the natural self-will ceased within Him—so too must a Christian (when he has truly become such) sell his own natural will for 20 pieces of silver. These are sold out of Christ’s 30 pieces of silver to become a servant of God in Christ, for the service and obedience of his Lord who lives within him. For his past years of "Adamite time" <note>This refers to the "old man" or the fallen state of humanity inherited from Adam, governed by natural impulses rather than the Spirit.</note> in this world are sold in and with Christ for 20 pieces of silver. Thus, the Adamite time of his natural will ceases in such a "selling" into Christ's suffering and death. He is then appointed by his Lord—who is risen from the dead within him and rules over death—as a steward <note>original: "Amptmann." An official or administrator in charge of an estate.</note> over Christ’s goods, to manage the same through Christ’s Spirit, as if in the power of his Lord who is in this world, according to that same Kingdom of Christ.

He is then cast into the "pits," representing the suffering and death of Christ. There, he loses his Adamic inheritance—his claim to the kingdom of this world—and is led away from it in his will and mind. There he must surrender his "father’s house"—meaning all his self-centeredness and his natural life—to his brothers in his father's house. That is to say, he must hand himself over to the power of God who governs this world. He must allow himself to be cast into the pit of the death of his own natural will, and there surrender himself to the death of Christ, being willing to die to the desires of this world (his Adamic house) and gladly suffering whatever his brothers of this world do to him.

8. Then, while he lies in the "pit of Christ" and has surrendered himself to Christ's death—being willing to leave everything for Christ’s sake and die to the death of his own will—Christ reveals His heart within him, signaling his resurrection from death. Christ makes him alive through His power and draws him out of the pit of death, just as Joseph was drawn out. He leads the person into His service, just as Joseph was led into the service of Pharaoh’s chief steward. From then on, everything within the person proceeds successfully, for Divine power governs him. He now receives Divine understanding and wisdom, and he knows how to manage his Master’s goods. This is what is meant by the Christian typology:

9. When a person becomes a Christian through such a process, they have surrendered everything—both their temporal goods and their own will—to God. God first leads the person into the image of Christ and makes them similar to Christ. However, God does not take away anything that the person previously held by natural right, such as the management of worldly goods. Instead, God takes away the power of the person's own nature—that is, the evil "self-will" which Adam introduced. Adam turned away from God and moved into a <term>creaturely selfhood</term> <note>original: "Creatürliche Selbheit." This refers to a state where a created being tries to be its own master, acting as if it were the center of the universe rather than a part of God's creation.</note> of his own wanting and working in earthly things. By doing this, Adam withdrew himself from the governance of God, his Lord, and claimed the essence of this world as his own property, as if he himself had created it. He no longer wished to be God’s servant or the caretaker of his <term>fellow-branches</term> <note>original: "Mitzweyge." An image derived from the vine and the branches (John 15), suggesting that all humans are branches of the same life-giving vine.</note>. He did not want to give them his power, will, and essence, but instead said: "Mine!" That is: "it is my own; I want to keep it for myself alone, and it shall rest in Me." He did not want to work through it for the life of his brothers, nor give them any of his life and strength; he even withdrew it from them

all of which are parables of His officials in the house of this world, how He

constructed kingdom built in their own lust for their own honor—and 
blot them out eternally from His countenance: but to the others, who had been 
faithful in His service, He gave full power over His house 
and also gave them the government and the pound of the one who had hidden 
it in the earth and had not wanted to carry out his commanded office.

### On Joseph’s Fear of God and Chastity.

30. Thus, it is well for all those in positions of power and office to consider that they should labor in God’s Office and be good stewards. They should not think only of how to strive for nobility and high status, nor how to fill their bellies and indulge their lusts with gluttony and drunkenness, nor how to unjustly wring the sweat <note>meaning the hard-earned labor or life-blood</note> from the wretched to gamble it away on their pride and banqueting, nor how to use force to squeeze and oppress the poor and the subordinates. All of these together are the evil officials and the murderers whom the Lord commanded to be put to death, and whose city He set ablaze with the fire of God’s wrath.

31. But now the world is full of such officials, to whom their Lord has long sent many messengers, yet they have only mocked and despised them. Therefore, the time of the Lord’s arrival is now at hand, for they have also now murdered His Son—the true reality of His Word—and have walked in pure self-indulgence; for this reason, these stewards must now give an account of their offices.

32. Further, Moses says of Joseph and speaks: "And it came to pass after these things that his master’s wife cast her eyes upon Joseph and said: Sleep with me." But he refused her and said to her: "Behold, my master takes no concern for what is in the house because of me, and everything he has, he has placed into my hands; and there is nothing so great in the house that he has hidden from me except for you, in that you are his wife. How then could I do such a great evil and sin against God?" And she spoke such words to Joseph daily, but he did not listen to her, to sleep near her or be around her. This is now the powerful image of how it goes with God’s children once they have attained the Divine Governance in the new rebirth <note>The spiritual transformation where a person is "born again" into a divine nature</note>, wherein they must now walk with their holy, blessed governance inside this house of flesh and Adamic prison; just as the soul has taken this unchaste whore-woman—the spirit of this world in animal desire—into marriage in flesh and blood. This whorish woman now stands against the chaste Joseph and constantly seeks to drive and pull him toward her dalliance, so that the new virginal child <note>The pure, spiritual part of the person created through rebirth</note> should again commit fornication with the animal whore, as Adam did—from which dalliance the earthly Eve arose for him, with whom he thereafter mated just like all the animals.

65. Whatever wills and runs for its own sake separates itself from the total Will of God and leads itself into <term>selfhood [Eigenheit]</term> <note>"Eigenheit" refers to the state of being focused on one's own ego or private desires rather than the universal divine flow.</note>, wherein there is no rest; for it must live in its own willing and running, and it is a vain unrest. 66. 67. For this is the torment of all the damned: that they *will*. That is, they will for selfhood, and in their willing, various forms are born, such as counter-willing or reluctance, where the wills are in conflict—where a single thing is manifest in many things at once. Therein the will becomes its own enemy. But when the will is only "One" with the eternal "One," then no enmity can exist within it, nor is there any possibility for enmity within it.

68. Therefore, this is the final <term>trial [Proba]</term> for man: when he stands still before God in all things, then a light arises for him out of the darkness, a life out of death, and a joy out of sadness. His prison became a joy to him, for he became a ruler over the prison while inside the prison; he was as a prisoner, and yet as a lord over the prisoners. He governed the prison and the prisoners and was a father and caregiver to the afflicted. His master took concern for nothing and was well pleased with whatever Joseph did, for in his eyes everything was pleasing and right.

69. For God's will does it within Himself, and all sin ceases. And even if God's wrathful-will moved within him and brought fire from heaven from the Lord (as with Elijah), everything is right before God; for the man does not do it, but God through him. He is the instrument through which God speaks and acts.

70. In this chapter, the Spirit presents a <term>figure [Figur]</term> <note>A "figure" is a symbolic pattern or a historical event that prefigures a spiritual reality.</note> of how the Spirit of God sees through the spirit of man, and how He leads the human spirit into "seeing" so that it can understand hidden things. For to explain dreams is nothing other than to see and understand the pattern—how the <term>Spirit of the World</term> <note>original: "Spiritus Mundi". This refers to the animating, astral soul of the physical cosmos that mediates between the divine and the material.</note> forms itself into a pattern within the human <term>constellation</term> <note>Böhme uses "constellation" to mean the internal spiritual and psychological makeup of a person, mirrored by the stars.</note> regarding those things which are already in effect in a person’s life. Or indeed, how they are formed into a pattern in the constellation through great conjunctions where the effect is not yet present, and yet is naturally imprinted. In this state, the human spirit, through Divine power, recognizes by the pre-image what kind of effect it shall have. This may also be understood through the diligent contemplation of <term>Astronomy</term> within <term>Astrology</term>, wherein the natural effect is prefigured—what is naturally worked and shaped through these celestial powers.

2. Because, however, Joseph was but a youth and had not studied such arts from the outside, it is to be understood that the Spirit of God led him with His "seeing" into the images of the dreams. The Spirit of God interpreted the dreams through Joseph's spirit, just as also happened with Daniel. For to interpret dreams is nothing else than to understand a magical image of the stars within a person's own property.

Because it is only an animal, it commonly leads the model into a fantastic image through its desire, and makes sorrow out of joy, and joy out of sorrow; but the soul is grieved in such a mirror and representation, from which great unrest often arises for the body.

6. But where a right and true vision occurs in a person, it happens through the "in-modeling" of the soul. When the soul, through its <term>Imagination</term> <note>For Böhme, "Imagination" is a potent, creative force that "images" or "models" spiritual reality into form.</note>, models itself into the figure, then the image stands in right human understanding. However, the Astral Spirit is constantly forming itself into earthly shapes, so that a completely perfect vision—as the work truly is in itself—rarely appears. Also, a person’s own daily imaginings often change the magical form, so that the figure corresponds to what he imagined during the day.

7. But the right visions are these: when the human will rests in God, then God is manifest in the human will. Then the soul sees with God's eyes from its innermost ground, where it stands within the Word of God. Then the "Speaking Word" goes with the soul into the magical image of the Constellation, and the Astral Spirit cannot model itself into the Phantasy, but must stand in the image and the figure exactly as the Constellation is. The Most High has prefigured what shall happen; thus, the **Word of God**, as the foundation of the soul, expresses the "figure" or image within the soul so that the soul understands it, just as Joseph and also Daniel expressed and interpreted it here. As soon as the figure of the vision was spoken to Joseph, the Spirit of God was present within the voice of the speaker and interpreted the vision within Joseph; for such are the Magical Visions <term>Magical Visions</term> <note>In Böhme’s writing, "Magical" refers to the creative power of the spirit and imagination to shape reality or perceive spiritual truths beyond the physical senses.</note> of all the prophets.

8. For after God appeared once to the prophets in an audible voice and called them to be prophets—as He did with Samuel—He appeared to them thereafter in Magical Visions and answered them regarding their questions.

<margin><unclear>C</unclear></margin>

9. The true prophetic foundation of magical seeing and understanding is this: Every prophet is a "goal" or mark in which a certain "Time" is enclosed. Thus, he is the mouth of that kingdom. That is to say, when that kingdom has awakened and given birth to the <term>Turba</term> <note>The "Turba" is a central concept in Böhme’s thought, referring to the "disturber" or the awakened wrath and chaos within nature that arises when it is out of harmony with the divine light.</note> within itself, the prophet is the mouth of the inner foundation. He is the one who speaks out the vanity within the Turba, and also the grace of God, which has had mercy upon human misery and resists the wrath of the Turba. That is: he reveals the awakened wrath of God and rebukes the kingdom for the sake of its vanity and idolatry, and comforts them again with the grace that has been turned toward them.

10. For his spirit stands in the "figure"—within the eternally-speaking Word of God from which life was first spoken and entered into a creature—having been turned back into an instrument of the Spirit of God. Through this instrument, the Spirit of God speaks and interprets. For the prophetic spirit could not, by its own power, interpret hidden future things if the Spirit of God did not see through him, and if the Word of God did not enter through his own word into the magical figure that the prophet sees.

11. For the prophet does not know that which he interprets beforehand by his own power; rather, when the Word models itself into the figure, the prophetic spirit sees through God’s own seeing how the Word of God passes through the figure. In that moment, the Word speaks the figure out through the prophetic spirit, as happened here with Joseph: when the King’s officers told him their dreams, the Word placed the figure of how things should go into Joseph’s understanding, so that Joseph recognized what their visions were.

12. Beforehand, however, he did not know it; but in the telling of the dream, the word of understanding modeled itself into Joseph’s understanding so that he knew it. For Joseph’s spirit stood in a magical figure turned back into the Word, in the same manner that the "New Birth" <note>The "New Birth" or "Regeneration" refers to the spiritual transformation of a person through Christ.</note> stands turned back into Christ’s Spirit. This was also the case with the other prophets, through whose mouths...

# Concerning the dreams of King Pharaoh: how Joseph was brought out of prison and set before the King, and attained great honors.

->Genesis 41<-

Moses says: and after two years, Pharaoh had a dream; and he stood by the water and saw seven beautiful, fat cows rise out of the water and go to pasture in the grass. After this, he saw seven other cows rise out of the water; these were ugly and lean, and they stood beside the cows on the riverbank. And the lean and ugly ones ate the seven beautiful, fat cows. Then Pharaoh awoke. And he fell asleep again and dreamed once more, and saw seven ears of grain growing out of one stalk, full and thick. After that, he saw seven thin and scorched ears sprout up, and the seven thin and scorched ears swallowed the seven thick and full ears. Then Pharaoh awoke and realized it was a dream. And when morning came, his spirit was troubled; he sent out and called for all the magicians <note>original: "Wahrsager," literally "truth-sayers" or "soothsayers." In the context of Egypt, these were the priestly scholars and dream interpreters.</note> in Egypt.

2. These dreams of Pharaoh were presented to him by God; therefore, no <term>Natural Magician</term> <note>original: "Magus Naturalis." In the author's context, this refers to a scholar or philosopher who studies the hidden laws and workings of the physical world.</note> or student of nature could interpret them. For the **Natural Magician** has power only within nature—only in that which nature forms through its own activity. He cannot reach into or give counsel regarding that which the Word of God models and forms. But the Prophet has the power to interpret it, for he is a **Divine Magician**, as Joseph is here.

3. Among the Egyptians, the **Magical Art** was common; but when it was turned into an abuse and into sorcery, it was rooted out. Nevertheless, it remained among the heathens until the Kingdom of Christ, until the **Divine Magic** <note>original: "Magia." Böhme uses this term to describe the creative, formative power of the spirit.</note> arose. Then, the natural magic perished among the Christians. In the beginning, it was well that it perished, for the heathen faith was extinguished along with it, and the magical images of nature—which they honored as gods—were thereby cleared out of human hearts.

4. But when the Christian faith became common, other "Magicians" arose, namely the sects within Christendom. These set themselves up as gods in place of the heathen idols and practiced a greater deceit than the heathens did with their magical images.

5. For the heathens looked toward the ground of nature’s ability and activity. These others, however, set themselves above the ground of nature, placing themselves merely in a <term>Historical Faith</term> <note>original: "Historischen Glauben." This refers to a belief based strictly on the literal, external record of scripture and dogma, lacking personal, internal spiritual experience.</note> where people were expected to believe whatever they invented.

Instead, there is only empty chatter about a supernatural magical ground, wherein they have installed themselves as idols and false gods. Yet they understand neither the **Divine** nor the **Natural Magic** <note>original: "Magiam."</note>, so that the world has become stone-blind through them. From this, the bickering and strife in faith has arisen; much is said about faith, with one person testifying to this and another to that, creating a heap of opinions. These are all worse than the heathen images, which at least had their basis in nature. But these images have no basis either in nature or in supernatural divine faith; rather, they are dumb idols, and their ministers are **servants of Baal**.

In Böhme's philosophy, faith is not just a thought, but a literal spiritual reality or "body."</note>. This substance is hidden from the outward eyes in visible man, just as the invisible God is hidden in the visible substance of this world.

10. The reason the **Natural Magicians** <note>original: "Magi Naturales." This refers to the deep spiritual core where the divine word interacts with the material world.</note>, which the heathen magicians did not understand. Their magical foundation in understanding was only in the effects and patterns of the stars and the elements. They did not understand the ground of **Eternal Nature**, from which the nature of this world has its origin and in which it stands. But Pharaoh's dreams drew their meaning from Eternal Nature and were placed through the Word of God as a visible image into the outward nature of time and into the outward form of man.

11. For the seven fat cows in the grass signify, in their inner ground, the seven properties of **Eternal Nature** <note>original: "ewigẽ Natur." The author's cosmological theory involves seven fundamental "source-spirits" or properties that constitute all of existence.</note> in the Holy, Good Being—as in the Kingdom of Heaven, where the Divine Power is substantial. And the seven lean, ugly, withered cows signify, in their inner ground, the seven properties of Eternal Nature in **God’s Wrath**, as in the Kingdom of Hunger and Thirst, where nature exists without the Divine Substance of God’s good power. The seven thick, fat, full ears of corn, as well as the seven withered, scorched ears, also signify the same thing.

# The 69th Chapter.

## How this famine went through all lands, and how Jacob sent his sons to the land of Egypt for grain, and how they came before Joseph, and how he behaved toward them, and what is to be understood by this?

->Genesis 42<-

This 42nd chapter of Genesis with Joseph and his brothers is now a figure <note>Böhme uses "figure" to mean a spiritual type or symbolic representation of a deeper reality.</note> of how God finally grants to such a converted Christian—who has had to enter into the process with Christ and has now overcome—his enemies also, who brought him into the process of Christ through their persecution and false betrayal; and how their sins are also set before their eyes, how they are also led into anguish and need, and how they are finally redeemed from pain and punishment out of pure grace, and how God becomes so merciful to them as they repent, and not only remits the punishment but also endows them with His blessing, just as Joseph does here to his brothers.

2. But alongside this, it is also presented in this figure how earnestly God shows Himself against sin—just as Joseph here against his brothers—and yet God is not earnest in wanting to punish the repentant sinner according to the full severity <note>Literally "according to the sharpness," meaning the strict letter of the law.</note>; but rather He acts harshly toward the soul in its conscience, so that sins may awaken and be recognized, and that the repentance may be all the greater, so that in such terror of sin, the person becomes humble and completely departs from sin and comes to loathe it, because he recognizes that sin contains such a terrible judgment within itself.

->The history reads thus:<-

3. When Jacob saw that grain was for sale in Egypt, he said to his sons, "Why do you look at one another for so long? Behold, I hear there is grain for sale in Egypt; go down and buy grain for us, that we may live and not die." Thus Joseph’s ten brothers went down to buy grain in Egypt. But Jacob did not let Benjamin, Joseph’s brother, go down with them, for he said: "Some accident might befall him."

4. This is now primarily a figure showing that when a person finds himself in the Divine wrath during such a famine—where he lacks righteousness—as Jacob did with his children in the famine: then the Father speaks in the

Before that, He gives his sinful brothers—that is, He first gives his terror into the conscience, and denies the comfort of His grace as the true Benjamin, Joseph's brother, in the face of the properties <note>Böhme uses "properties" (Eigenschafften) to describe the specific spiritual qualities or driving forces within a person's nature.</note> of sins; and He sends the properties of sins—those in which the sins were committed—to buy such grain from Joseph, as from Christ, according to grace.

6. The sinner must apply himself to it, and with earnestness enter into the suffering and death of Christ, and die away from his sins before grace in the **prison of God’s wrath**, and cast himself upon Joseph's—as upon Christ's—mercy for grace; not merely standing outside and saying: "With Christ, grace is for sale," and tickling and comforting oneself with grace. No, that does not refresh the poor soul; you must go down into Egypt to your offended brother, whom you have cast into the pit within yourself through your sins, and you must step before his eyes in great humility, even though you will not recognize him at first, until he makes himself known to you in his mercy. There, you must buy grain for the poor soul in Christ’s power and glory, which he attained in his **resurrection**, so that the soul may live and not die, just as Jacob said to his children.

But Joseph was the regent in the land and sold grain to all the people in the land. When his brothers now came to him, they fell down before him to the earth on their faces, and he looked at them and recognized them, but he acted as a stranger toward them and spoke harshly to them, and said to them: "Where do you come from?" They said, "From the land of Canaan, to buy food." But although he knew them, they did not know him.

8. This is now the first state when the poor soul turns to Christ to fetch food from him; thus He stands before the soul in its will, entering fully into its essence <term>essence: original "Essenz." In Böhme's philosophy, this refers to the fundamental spiritual substance or "being" of a person.</term>, to see if the free will has directed itself toward Him. 9. Then Christ looks into them and indeed grasps them with the severe bond of God's wrath, but His love and grace only hide themselves within it. It is these [love and grace] which rebuke the poor sinner for his sins and trouble him, so that he is terrified and fears God. When the soul stands and calls out to God, Christ says in the conscience: "Who are you? Just look at yourself, whether you are even worthy of me?" Just as Joseph did here when he said: "Who are you?" and acted harshly and like a stranger.

10. And Joseph remembered the dreams he had dreamed of them, and said to them: "You are spies, and have come to see where the land is open." That is, Christ remembers His mercy and His bitter suffering and death, and says to the soul: "You are a spy, and you come to me only wanting to see where the gates of my grace are open; but that shall not help you. You must go about it differently; you must first enter through the gates of my suffering and death. Otherwise, you are merely a spy, wanting to see if the gates of my grace stand open so that you might cover yourself with them as a cloak <note>original: "Deckmantel." This implies using the idea of God's forgiveness as a superficial excuse to keep sinning without changing one's heart.</note>. You must be in earnest; for you only wish to be my betrayer and carry my grace in your mouth."

11. And Joseph’s brothers answered him and said: "No, my lord; your servants have come to buy food. We are all the sons of one man; we are honest, and your servants have never been spies." In the figure <note>The "figure" refers to the symbolic representation: the biblical story as a mirror of the internal spiritual process.</note>, this means that before the properties of the soul truly recognize themselves in their vanity, when the wrath of God steps before their eyes—as if into their very essence <term>Essentien: the underlying spiritual substances or "being" of a person</term>—the soul thinks it is being treated unjustly. For it thinks that if it comforts itself with the merit of Jesus Christ and believes in Christ—that He is God's Son and has paid for the soul—then it cannot be scolded as a divine spy and an unjust hypocrite. It thinks it is already righteous through Christ's justification because it believes this was done for its benefit.

12. But just as Joseph said to his brothers: "No; but you have come to see where the land is open," so also the Spirit of Christ accuses the soul's essences. For He tests them [to see] that they are not yet shattered and still have their own desire within them, and only want to reach for grace immediately as if for an open gate. This does not count for the soul; it must first enter into Christ's suffering and death, and first put these on through earnest repentance and the conversion <note>original: "Vmbkehrung." Literally a "turning around," describing the fundamental shift of the human will away from the self and toward God.</note> of its will. Only then may it enter through the open gates—through Christ's wounds and death—into His resurrection.

❧ ...not of an **historically accepted faith** or mere appearance, but **essentially**, as the branch on the vine: you must be a branch on the tree; you must live in the life of Christ; you must have his flesh and blood actually and essentially in your inward ground <note>Böhme’s "inward ground" (*inwendiger Grund*) refers to the deepest, most fundamental level of the human soul where the divine can reside.</note>, and be Christ; otherwise, you are all together nothing but **spies**, researchers, and **historical Christians** <note>Böhme frequently critiqued "historical Christians" who believed the Bible as a factual history book but lacked a personal, mystical connection to the living Spirit.</note>, and no better than Jews, Turks, and Heathens.

❧ 22. 23. Gape no longer, it is time: She is truly born; your redemption approaches: The Bridegroom calls his Bride; yes, you must enter into Joseph's prison in this famine, if you do not want <insert>to perish</insert>. Amen.

25. When the soul approaches God and wants to do penance, but its inward ground is still entirely locked in vanity—so that the **mind** still clings to its own selfhood <term>Eigenheit</term> <note>Selfhood or "ownness" is Böhme’s term for the egoistic will that separates the soul from God.</note>—but if the soul will not desist from penance, and yet cannot yet be rid of earthly desire, and remains in prayer, then God the Father lets the soul's essence out of the prison of his **wrath** <note>In Böhme’s system, the "Wrath" is the dark, fiery power of God that consumes the soul if it is not tempered by Love.</note>, so that the mind feels well again, like one who has been released from prison; then the mind also says, "I have become quite well in my prayer and this penance."

26. For God's wrath has let nature out of its prison, so that it should press toward God with great labor: for in its prison it cannot; for it is anxious and sees only its committed sins, which always drive it back, so that it fears God and is ashamed. 27. But the wrath of God still holds them ever by a bond, just as Joseph kept one brother prisoner until they brought him the last brother as well: Thus must the poor soul remain standing in a bond of the imprisonment of death, until it pours out the last brother—as the innermost ground <note>original: "inwendigsten Grundt." 28. Then, when this earnestness enters into <term>practice</term> <note>Böhme uses "practice" to mean the actual lived application of faith, rather than mere intellectual study.</note> so that God recognizes it is earnest, then the last brother is also released; that is, the last bond of the wrath of God is loosened. But meanwhile, before it happens thus, the soul must lie captive in a bond.

29. But nonetheless, God speaks to the other released forms of life <note>original: "Lebens Gestältnüssen." ### How this famine went through all lands.

when I wish to turn to God and perform <term>repentance</term> <note>original: "Busse." In Böhme’s theology, this is not just saying sorry, but a total "turning around" or transformation of the soul’s direction.</note>, now his sighs and tears hold me back, which I have forced out of him for my pleasure, mockery, and vanity; now I stand here, and the heaven becomes as iron in my conscience.

32. Then God speaks in the conscience: "You surely knew it; for that reason I let my Word be spoken to you. You knew well that you were doing wrong, but your evil wantonness had to rule. Now you want to have grace?" And the devil speaks: "It is in vain; the grace is gone; heaven is closed; hell is open; just give up, you will achieve nothing."

33. But the great mercy in the grace of Christ in the inward <term>ground</term> <note>Böhme uses "ground" (Grund) to refer to the deepest, most essential part of the human spirit where it meets the Divine.</note> presses through with his misery and great pity, although she [Grace] still hides her face of love for now, so that the soul does not recognize her. This makes the troubled soul full of misery, so that she flees and weeps within herself before God, and confesses herself guilty of all malice; and in such kindled misery she begins to bitterly complain of and repent for her sins. She is also so full of shame before Christ's eyes that she hides her face before God and does not know what to do for misery. For she sees within herself with her own eyes that she binds and holds God's strict justice in her trembling, just as Joseph's brothers had to see that their brother was bound before their eyes for the sake of their sins.

34. For although Christ is active in the soul's essence in the inward ground of the incorporated grace, and thus shatters it so that it sees and repents its sin, he still presents himself as quite foreign toward the soul and will not touch it with any ray of love—just as Joseph acted like a stranger as if he did not understand their language and spoke to them through an interpreter.

35. It is that very same interpreter who brings the soul into such repentance; otherwise it could not. For the soul has nothing more in its own power than this: that it may turn its <term>fathomless</term> <note>original: "vngründlichen." This refers to the root of the human will which arises from the "Unground" or the abyss of God's own being.</note> supernatural will toward God, as if back into that from which it came, and stand still there; which is very difficult for it, yet possible. Unless its will has broken itself off entirely from the incorporated gate of grace and surrendered to the devil's poison, so that the will of the soul's <term>Unground</term> <note>original: "Vngrundes." A central Böhme term for the absolute, fathomless "nothing" or source from which all existence originates.</note> has entered into the figure of a false thistle and become entirely poisonous; then it is difficult and reaches no repentance, but is frivolous and hardened, and never desires to turn around. Such a soul does not repent any malice, but rejoices in it as long as it bears the body; then it is all over for it. But where there is still a tiny spark of divine desire, there is still counsel.

### ...and how Jacob sent his sons into the land of Egypt, etc.

<margin>Chapter 69</margin>
36. And Moses speaks further: And Joseph gave command that their sacks be filled with grain and their money be returned, each into his own sack, and also provisions for the way; and so it was done for them. And they loaded their goods onto their donkeys and departed from there; but when one of them opened his sack to give his donkey fodder in the inn, he became aware of his money, for it lay at the top of the sack, and he said to his brothers: "My money has been returned to me; see, it is here in my sack!" Then their hearts failed them and they were terrified one with another, and said: "Why has God done this to us?"

37. This is now the lovely **figure** of how God takes nothing from the <term>repentant sinner</term> <note>original: "bußfertigen Sünder." For Böhme, repentance is a literal "turning about" of the soul’s will from the world back toward God.</note> when he surrenders everything in his will and thinks only to remain steadfast in God. He takes no gift nor anything else from him; He also does not take his temporal goods, if only he surrenders them to God and abandons <term>me-ness</term> <note>original: "Meinheit." This is a central term in Böhme’s thought, referring to the selfish ego or the desire to "own" oneself and one's possessions rather than existing in a state of yieldedness to God.</note>. Then God fills his sack and gives him back the money—which he gives to the poor and miserable in his blessing—all of it, and lays it at the top of his nourishment so that the person sees that God has bestowed it upon him again in His wondrous blessing.

38. Because of this, a person often marvels at how it happens that temporal nourishment falls to him in such a miraculous way, even though he did not seek it so or know anything of it. And he is even terrified by it, wondering if he should accept it; he may even think it happens to him as a temptation, just as Joseph's brothers thought here. Joseph tested them in this way so that he might have a cause <note>That is, a legal or moral reason to test their character further.</note> with them.

39. This is also indicative of the inward gift of Christ: that when the poor sinner pours out his heart before God as payment for grace, and gives God whatever he has, God fills the sack of his heart with the grace of Christ and gives him good provisions—such as understanding and wisdom—for the path of his **pilgrimage**, as he must travel through this <term>vale of tears</term> <note>original: "Jammerthal." A common poetic term for the earthly world, seen as a place of exile and sorrow compared to the heavenly homeland.</note> back home to his Fatherland.

<margin>End</margin>
40. But during this journey on this pilgrimage path, while the <term>Adamic man</term> <note>The "Adamish" (Adamisch) man refers to our fallen, earthly nature inherited from Adam, which must eventually pass away.</note> has his sack filled with heavenly goods, that which belongs to the kingdom of God's wrath (as well as the earthly world) is stolen away from him, as is seen in this figure.

41. For when Jacob's sons came home to their father and told him how it had gone with them, and emptied their sacks and found the money again, and also wanted to have Benjamin with them in Egypt, Jacob said: "You are robbing me of my children; Joseph is no longer here, Simeon is no longer there, and you want to take Benjamin away; everything is going against me."

<sig>Gggg 3</sig>

# How Jacob’s sons requested Benjamin from him.

42. Here stands **Jacob**, their father, in the figure of the outer nature’s **selfhood** <note>original: "Eygenheit." This refers to the soul's egoistic attachment to itself and its own desires.</note>; we see how nature complains when it is robbed of its rights and what it has brought forth into the light. This stands as a remarkably beautiful figure; for the outer nature speaks when it sees the divine gifts within itself—by which it loses the right of its selfhood—and says: "I am being robbed of my power." **Joseph**, as the internal ground of the Kingdom of Heaven which I had in Paradise, is no longer present; and now this gift also wants to take my authority, represented by my children—that is, the properties of my nature. Everything is going against me; I must allow myself to be robbed.

43. But **Reuben** spoke to his father: "If I do not bring **Benjamin** back to you, then strangle my two sons; give him into my hand, I will bring him back to you." This means that God comforts nature and says: "Give me your forms <note>original: "Geſtältnuß." In Böhme's thought, these are the fundamental qualities or "spirit-shapes" that make up a being.</note>, which are your children, into my hand. I will only lead them into Egypt to **Joseph**—that is, to **Jesus**—and will give them back to you. You shall lose nothing; if not, then kill my two sons in you—that is, kill the first and second <term>Principle</term>." <note>Böhme’s "Principles" are the fundamental dimensions of reality: the First is the dark fire-power, the Second is the light/love of God, and the Third is the physical world.</note>

44. Which would indeed happen if nature were robbed of its forms: the Kingdom of God in Love, and also the Kingdom of God in the **fire-power**, would have to cease within the nature of man. In this way, the Spirit of God plays very secretly in the figure of the **rebirth**. Reason will look upon this explanation as something foreign, but we know what we are writing here, understood by those who are ours <note>Böhme often addresses a small circle of "initiated" spiritual seekers, contrasting their insight with "Reason" (Vernunft), which he sees as limited and worldly logic.</note>.

45. And **Jacob** said: "My son **Benjamin** shall not go down with you, for his brother is dead and he alone is left. If a mishap should befall him on the way upon which you travel, you would bring my gray hair with heartache into the grave." This means that nature is timid <note>original: "blöde." In 17th-century German, this meant weak, shy, or fearful rather than unintelligent.</note> when it is meant to enter into the death of Christ; it fears dying and wants nothing to do with it. It excuses itself because of the loss of its heavenly **Joseph**, the heavenly image; because nature cannot comprehend this, it says: "It is dead." If harm were now to come to these forms of my life on this path, I would have to

->dissolve with heartache, and my life would<-
->come to an end.<-

# Chapter 70.

## How Jacob’s sons travel back to Egypt to Joseph for grain because of the famine, taking Benjamin with them; how Joseph had them led into his house and served food from his table: what is to be understood by this.

->Genesis 43.<-

This entire chapter **prefigures** <note>original: "præfiguriret." To Böhme, biblical events are "types" or shadows of the internal spiritual process of the soul.</note> for us the beautiful image of how the outward nature first acts in such a process. When it must surrender its will so that its **life-essence** may enter into Egypt—that is, into the **Death of Christ**—it is quite dull and timid; yet finally, it consents, so that all its life-forms may enter into the dying of their **selfhood** <note>original: "selbheit." Böhme uses this term to describe the ego-driven, fallen nature of man that resists God's will.</note>, as if into the true Egypt, through divine trust, so that the will of God may lead them into it.

2. And then, it shows how the life-forms are afraid before **Joseph**—that is, before **God’s countenance**—because they feel an evil conscience within themselves. Just as Jacob’s sons were afraid of Joseph, for they constantly thought God would punish them because of Joseph, which made them tremble.

3. And thirdly, it shows how God first deals so kindly with the forms of the **soulish nature** <note>The "soulish nature" refers to the psychological and vital aspects of the human being that must be transformed.</note> and first gives them **Heavenly Bread** from His own Being, yet still in a "foreign" form; just as Joseph invited his brothers as guests and fed them from his table, so that they ate and drank and became merry, and he let them depart in peace. But immediately after, he came with a terrible temptation by having his cup placed in Benjamin’s sack, chasing after them and bringing them back. All of this stands powerfully as a figure of the **penitent sinner**; how it goes with him until God gives Himself to be known in Love.

4. **Moses’** words follow thus: "The famine, however, pressed upon the land; and when they had consumed the grain they had brought from Egypt, their father said to them: 'Go back again and buy us a little food.' Then **Judah** answered him and said: 'The man strictly charged us, saying: "You shall not see my face unless your brother is with you." If you will now send our brother with us, we will go down and buy food for you to eat. But if you do not send him, we will not go down; for the man said to us: "You shall not see my face unless your brother is with you."'"

<meta>catchword: The</meta>

<summary>Böhme interprets the return of Jacob's sons to Egypt as an allegory for the soul's fearful but necessary surrender to God's will, where Joseph represents the hidden presence of Christ.</summary>

28. O you poor old **Jacob** of "spying" Christendom! Do let your hungry sons, who are quite thin from the great hunger in their conscience, go to Joseph. 40. Comfort is only this: that a Christian consoles himself that through such repentance in CHRIST JESUS, he will attain a gracious God; and this shall also be his very comfort, so that he does not despair.

41. The satisfaction <note>satisfaction: the theological concept that Christ’s death paid the debt of human sin</note> with which the unrighteous person comforts himself, saying: "My works count for nothing, Christ has done it all, I can do nothing"; and yet remains in sin under such "comfort"—that is precisely the Devil’s fishing net, with which he catches his fish by using Christ’s mantle as a lure.

42. Christ wore only the purple robe while he stood in his suffering; but when he hung upon the Cross, he no longer had it, and much less so in his Resurrection. Thus, a person should only take up this mantle when he enters into repentance through Christ’s suffering and death; in repentance alone is it valid, and nowhere else. It is for the poor soul to wrap itself in it when it feels shame for its sins before the face of God.

43. Everything that teaches or believes otherwise is deceit, fable, and Babel <note>Babel: a term Böhme frequently uses to describe the confusion and vanity of the institutionalized, "fallen" church</note>. All teachers who teach otherwise are merely servants of the belly and of the Devil’s fishermen, and a deception of the world; let a person beware of them. For whoever wishes to be a teacher must also be a true Christian, so that he may also live in Christ; otherwise, he is the thief and murderer who climbs into the sheepfold by another way, of whom Christ speaks.

44. And Moses speaks further: "Then they took the gifts and double the money with them, and Benjamin, and set out and went down to Egypt, and stood before Joseph. When Joseph saw them with Benjamin, he said to his steward: 'Lead these men into the house, and slaughter and prepare a meal; for they shall eat with me at noon.' And the man did as Joseph had told him, and led the men into Joseph’s house."

45. This means that the concealer <note>the "concealer" refers to the part of the human ego that tries to hide its sins or true nature</note> must come out from under the mantle and return his ill-gotten goods, and step before the face of the Heavenly Joseph, coming naked and bare with his "selfhood" <term>Ichheit</term> <note>Ichheit (I-ness): Böhme’s term for the self-centered ego or the individual will that separates itself from God</note>, or his own abilities, and bringing the "true Benjamin" within him. Then Joseph approaches him and looks upon him, and commands his steward—as the Spirit of Power—to lead these people into his house, which is into his humanity. There, the Lamb of God shall be prepared, and this person—or the life-essences of the righteous soul—shall eat with Joseph at his table at "noon." (This "noon" refers to the high Light of Grace, when the Light shines in the soul at midday). And here Joseph’s brothers are reconciled, when they eat of his food with Joseph, that is, with Christ.

# How Jacob’s Sons, on Account of the Famine <note>original: "Thewrung," referring to the great famine in Egypt described in the Book of Genesis.</note>

46. **This** is the Lord’s Supper of Revelation 22. Here one enters the path of man and becomes a brother of Joseph, and no longer needs to be comforted from the outside, but rather becomes a Christian in Christ—one who has died to their sins with Christ, and has become alive in Him, and has risen in Him, and lives with Him, eats with Him at His table, and is no longer a servant of sin, nor must they be afraid anymore; rather, they are a son in the house to whom the inheritance belongs, according to the power of the Scriptures.

47. **And** as Joseph’s steward <term>steward: in German, "Haußhalter," one who manages a household; Böhme uses this figure to represent the various ways God’s grace or ministers guide the soul</term> had led them into Joseph’s house, they were still afraid and spoke with him at the door concerning the money they had found in their sacks. But he comforted them and said: "I have received your money; your God has thus bestowed a treasure upon you in your sacks." and he led Simeon out to them, and led them into Joseph’s house, and gave them water so that they might wash their feet, and gave their donkeys fodder. They, however, prepared the gift until Joseph came at noon; for they had heard that they were to eat bread there.

48. **This** is now the figure <term>figure: a symbolic representation or "type" from the Bible that points to a spiritual reality</term> of the troubled person who now enters Joseph’s house. When they have committed much wrong and have nothing to give back, they return it with their heart before Joseph’s house in true confession and acknowledgment, and would gladly return it with their hands if they only had the power to do so. To this person, Joseph’s steward says: "Do not be afraid anymore; I have already received it in your repentance." Christ has paid and restored it for you in His blood. Thus, when all that is gone and nothing more remains, and you are in poverty and misery, keep the little that you have to sustain your life; even if you hold it unrighteously <note>Böhme is addressing the anxiety of a repentant person who cannot physically undo every past financial or social sin because they are now destitute.</note> and should have nothing of your own in this world, God has nonetheless bestowed a treasure upon you. Take water and wash your feet—that is: cleanse the conduct of your hands and feet, and do no more evil, and do not keep what is unrighteous, but only the little that you still hold rightly, so that you cannot [be expected to] pay back the unrighteousness [beyond your means].

49. **This** is not to be understood as meaning that one should not want to restore what was taken through usury <note>original: "Wucher," meaning excessive interest or dishonest gain.</note> from their own possessions if they are able to do so. We are speaking of the poor person who has nothing left but a piece of bread for their life. No pretense <note>original: "einschlieff," likely a variant of "Einschleichen" or a reference to a deceptive excuse.</note> is valid before God; the conscience must have become pure, or you are a thief. For the figure stands here as well: the steward had also given fodder to their donkeys. This refers to the earthly body, which Christ wishes to provide with fodder and food through His stewards.

58. This figure is now the most secret foundation and the highest mystery between God and man. Although it outwardly appears as if Joseph merely wanted to hide himself from his brothers—that he too was a Hebrew by descent—yet the Spirit has here presented such a deep mystery that no Reason <note>Böhme uses "Vernunfft" (Reason) to describe the limited, worldly intellect that cannot understand spiritual truths without divine illumination.</note> can perceive it.

59. For in this place, Joseph stands in the figure of Christ, who has a special food (of which they know nothing), as can be seen at Jacob’s Well when his disciples urged him to eat. There he said: *He had a food of which they knew nothing,* that he might do the will of him who sent him; for the faith of the pagan woman <note>A reference to the Samaritan woman at the well in John 4.</note> was his food.

60. Christ, according to the eternal Word of the Deity, does not eat of the bread of heaven like a creature. Rather, man’s faith and earnest prayer, and the soul’s praise of God, is his food. This the eternal Word, which became man, eats as something special that belongs to no other human nor any other creature, and which they cannot eat. And in that he eats the faith and prayer, together with the praise of God from our souls, so human faith, prayer, and praise become substantial <term>substantial: "wesentlich," meaning they take on a real, spiritual form or "essence" (Wesen).</term> in the Word of Power. It is then one essence with the nature of the heavenly corporeality of Christ—all of it being the one body of Christ: at once God and Essence. As God, Man, and Essence, they are entirely one.

61. This Essence—which is one essence with his humanity assumed from us, in which he shed his blood, and which is at once Divine and Human essence, as supernatural flesh and blood—he now gives back to human faith to eat and drink (excepting the error <note>original: "Jrrigkeit," referring to the fallen or sinful tendency of our biological nature.</note> of our humanity).

Here, he explores the union of the soul with the divine through the metaphor of eating and drinking.</meta>

<margin>Chapter 70</margin>

62. For faith, in its hungry desire, is the mouth that receives and takes it in. Through this impression, grasping, or taking in, faith eats Christ's flesh and blood. This eating and drinking is enclosed and preserved within the inner <term>Paradise Image</term><note>Böhme refers to the "Paradise Image" as the original, holy spiritual form of humanity that existed before the Fall of Adam.</note>, which faded in Adam but becomes alive again in Christ. There, the human paradisical essence and Christ's flesh and blood are entirely one being and remain so eternally. This inner person is no longer called Adam, but Christ, as a member of the body and essence of Christ, within which is the temple of the Holy Spirit. God’s holy Word is present there <term>substantially</term><note>original: "wesentlich"; in Böhme’s theology, this means something is not just a concept, but has a real, spiritual "body" or substance.</note>, and it is a form of the un-imagined Godhead, existing as the formed Word of God—an image of God.

63. This is precisely the <term>figure</term><note>A "figure" is a symbolic representation or an allegory found in the Bible.</note> shown by Joseph being served separately, and his brothers also separately: that there is still a distinction between Christ and his food, and between man and his food. This distinction is not according to the creaturely humanity of Christ that comes from us, but rather according to the unformed, eternally-speaking Word within him, in which the whole of God is active and generative—not locked inside, but speaking out in full omnipotence, not as a creature, but as God.

64. In us humans, however—to the extent that a person possesses the essence of God and Christ within themselves—the Word is formed and substantial. And this formed, substantial Word eats again from the formed Word of God, as if from Christ’s flesh and blood, within which the unformed Word dwells along with the entire fullness of the Godhead.

65. Yet this does not belong to the human creature in its own possession or self-hood as it does in Christ Jesus; rather, the human is a vessel and dwelling house of God. This happens in the same way as when fire possesses a piece of iron and glows through it so that it is entirely "fiery," yet the iron does not possess the fire in its own power or authority—for if the fire is extinguished, the iron remains a dark iron. Or, it is like how the sun penetrates a plant and draws it upward, becoming substantial within the plant, yet the sun’s spirit remains only a power within the plant, and the body of the plant does not actually become the sun. This is how the relationship between God and man is to be understood.

66. Furthermore, when Moses says: *And they served the Egyptians separately as well, for the Egyptians may not eat bread with the Hebrews,* this also has its symbolic meaning. While it may have been true outwardly in history that they were not permitted to eat together—a fact we leave unchallenged in its own value, just as we leave the rest of the history as it stands—we wish only to interpret the meaning of why the Spirit of God had it recorded so precisely.

<summary>Böhme explains the mystical union between the soul and Christ using the metaphor of a meal, clarifying that while the soul "eats" the divine essence, it remains a vessel for God rather than becoming God itself.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Böhme’s mystical commentary on the story of Joseph in Egypt (Genesis 43). Böhme is using the scene of Joseph dining with his brothers to explain how different types of people—believers, non-believers, and those who are Christian in name only—interact with the "food" of the Divine Word and the Body of Christ.</meta>

### How Joseph's Sons [Dealt] with the Famine

67. Now, if we wish to investigate this, we must consider the <term>natural Adamic man</term><note>The "Adamic man" refers to humanity in its fallen state, governed by natural logic and earthly desires rather than spiritual rebirth.</note>, regardless of his race or name—be he Heathen, Turk <note>In the 17th century, "Turk" was the common term for Muslims.</note>, or a mere <term>Titular Christian</term><note>A "Titular Christian" is someone who is Christian in name only, following the outward rituals without an inner spiritual transformation.</note>, or a Jew. In this regard, they are all alike; none is different from the other. All of these are not permitted to eat with a true Christian, just as the Egyptians could not eat with Joseph’s brothers. Why? Because they have no mouth for such food; their mouths are still closed to it. They cannot enjoy the <term>substance</term><note>original: "wesentliche"; Böhme uses this to mean something that has a real, spiritual body or presence, not just a symbolic idea.</note> of Christ’s body. It is an abomination to them, and they feel a loathing for it. We see this today: to the Jews, Turks, and Heathens, it is a gruesome thing when a Christian says, "He eats Christ's flesh and drinks his blood."

68. Likewise, it is now an abomination to "Titular Christendom." One party does not believe in the <term>substantial</term> partaking of Christ’s body, but wishes to have it only "spiritually" <note>This likely refers to the Reformed/Zwinglian view that the Eucharist is purely symbolic.</note>. The other party wishes to fill the mouth of the natural Adamic man and grasp it with physical teeth <note>This refers to a literalist or "Capernaitic" view of the Eucharist.</note>. In neither party is there true knowledge or understanding. They sit at the table like Joseph’s ignorant brothers who did not recognize Joseph; faith eats, but their rational understanding does not recognize Joseph in his meal.

69. So <term>Reason</term><note>In Böhme’s writing, "Reason" (Vernunfft) is often the villain—the limited, logical mind that tries to understand God without spiritual illumination.</note> speaks: "Because the Jews, Turks, and ignorant Heathens have no mouth for such food, and Christ says, 'He who does not eat the flesh of the Son of Man has no life in him,' then they must all be damned." O Israel, how blind you are here! You know as little of this as they do, or as little as Joseph’s brothers knew of Joseph.

70. The Turks, Jews, and foreign peoples—whose desire and prayer go toward the one God—do indeed have a mouth, but not in the same way as a "right" Christian. For as the desire is the mouth, so is the food within the mouth. They desire the Spirit of God; thus they eat, in the same manner as Christ’s humanity exists in the Father and the Son.

71. A true Christian, however, has an *incarnate* mouth. That is: the desire of the soul—or rather, the substantial Christ, acting as the <term>Virgin Sophia</term><note>Sophia (Divine Wisdom) is a central figure in Böhme’s thought, representing the mirror of God and the spiritual bride of the soul.</note>—has a mouth for the <term>substantial Word</term>. Those others have a mouth for the *un-substantial* Word: they desire the attribute of God the Father, the "One God," and they receive Him too. But here, Grace is not yet fully revealed to them.

72. But because the Father has given all people to His Son, Christ (as Christ Himself says), and has revealed His Grace in Christ, He accepts everyone only in Christ, and there is no salvation outside of Christ. Therefore, the Father gives to the Son the earnest, calling prayers [of those other peoples]. Christ receives these from His Father, takes them into Himself, and "eats" them. He fulfills them with His humanity, His death, and His shed blood. Thus, they are substantially present in Christ through their spirit, even though it remains hidden within them.

He distinguishes between a merely symbolic or a crudely physical understanding of the Eucharist, favoring a mystical, "substantial" union.</summary>

73. For they do not desire the flesh of the Son of Man; therefore, in their <term>selfhood</term><note>original: "selbheit"; Böhme’s term for the egoistic state of separation from God, where the human will acts independently of the divine will.</note>, they have no mouth for Christ's flesh and blood, as they have no desire for it. Yet, in their spirit, they are <term>substantially</term><note>original: "wesentlich"; Böhme uses this to describe something that has a real, spiritual presence or "body," rather than being just a thought or symbol.</note> in Christ. However, their inner paradisiacal humanity—which faded in Adam and within which the <term>embodied grace</term><note>original: "eingeleibte Gnade"; the divine potential or "spark" placed within humanity by God in the Garden of Eden.</note> lies hidden in Paradise—remains concealed from them and without an active life.

74. For Christ does not dwell <term>substantially</term> within them as he does in a true Christian. The essence of their faith, however, is hidden in Christ until the day of restoration for that which was lost in Adam. At that time, their <term>Paradise-image</term>, which is not revealed in this life, will put on the essence of their faith through God's bestowed grace—which extends from one to all—derived from Christ’s Spirit. For that same embodied grace, as the <term>spoken-in Word</term><note>original: "eingesprochene Wort"; Böhme refers to God speaking the Word into the human soul at creation and again as a promise of redemption.</note>, also stands within them and yearns for Christ’s substance.

75. But because their <term>essentiality</term> in the Word exists in Christ outside of this place—since Christ fulfills their faith in God within himself—their essential faith in God will also put on the <term>spoken-in Word</term> in the Paradise-image, along with the same in the revelation of **JESUS** Christ, and thereby the whole person.

76. For the Scripture says: *By grace you have been saved, and that not of yourselves, not through your own knowledge, but through God’s mercy.* <note>Böhme is paraphrasing Ephesians 2:8-9.</note> It does not depend on knowledge—as if knowledge could "take" or "grasp" Christ—but it depends on the giving, that is, on the grace which gives Christ to the ignorant in their faith in God, just as it does to the knowing in their desire. For both, it happens through grace.

77. For Adam went out from the one God into a <term>selfhood</term>, into ignorance, and led us all with him into that same ignorance. But grace came again from that same one God and offers itself to all the ignorant—to the Heathen as well as the Jew.

78. Among the Jews, however, the image of grace stood in the <term>figure</term><note>original: "Figur"; Böhme uses this to refer to the Old Testament types or shadows—rituals and laws—that pointed toward the coming of Christ.</note> of how grace intended to receive humanity again. Now, the "fathers of the figure"—the Jews—had no more share in grace than those among whom the image had not been revealed, for the <term>prefiguration</term><note>original: "Fürbilde"; a prototype or shadow-image of the truth to come.</note> looked toward Christ. Through their faith and prayer, the Jews pressed through the prefiguration into the one grace that was in God, which God bestowed upon Adam and his children. But the Heathen, who did not have the Law and yet believed in the one promised grace of God without circumcision, pressed into grace without the prefiguration.

# How Jacob's Sons because of the Famine
