79. For the ability was given to one people just as to the other; no people could do anything of their own accord, but Grace took the will for the ability and gave them equal power: to the Jews as to the believing <term>Heathens</term><note>original: "Heyden"; referring to non-Jewish, non-Christian nations of antiquity.</note>. But unbelief and the lack of will were the damnation for both the Jews and the Heathens, because they kept their will in <term>selfhood</term><note>original: "selbheit"; Böhme’s term for the egoistic state of separation from God, where the human will acts independently of the divine will.</note> and obstinacy, and went whoring after other idols. Thus, it was not circumcision and the sacrifices that were the salvation of the Jews, but rather Grace, which presented itself through such figures pointing toward the humanity of Christ; Grace intended to fulfill the figure, and this future fulfillment was their salvation.

80. So also now, the Christians have the figure of Grace under the Gospel in its fulfillment. They cannot take this fulfillment by their own power; rather, the fulfillment of Grace offers itself to them. If they are willing to surrender themselves into it, then a "mouth" is given to them to receive that Grace.

81. The others, however, direct their will toward the Grace of God—which is the very same Grace the Christians have, and nothing else—but they do not know the <term>substantial</term><note>original: "wesentlich"; Böhme uses this to describe something that has a real, spiritual presence or "body," rather than being just an abstract concept.</note> Grace in the image of fulfillment. Yet Grace takes their will along with their desire into itself, and gives the desire a "mouth" within Grace, which remains hidden from the creature until the Day of the Revelation of Jesus Christ.

82. Therefore, there is no other difference between them than the substantial movement in the <term>Paradise-image</term><note>original: "Paradeyß-Bilde"; the original, holy spiritual form of humanity that was lost in the Fall but remains as a hidden potential for restoration.</note>, where the Paradise-image has not yet "put on" Christ in substance as it has in true Christians. And yet, faith in the Grace of God in Christ is substantial—not as a human possession, but in God, who fulfills all things and is present and dwells through all. Thus, the substantial Grace is near to believing Jews and <term>Turks</term><note>In the 17th century, "Turks" was the standard term for Muslims.</note>, but within them, it remains ungrasped by their creaturely nature.

83. They have Christ within them, but they do not grasp him; their will then enters into the substantial Grace of Christ, and Christ is revealed in their nature just as he is in Christians. For Grace in Christ is bestowed upon the believing Jews and other peoples, for it hovers through them, and their will toward God is within it and walks within it.

84. A <term>nominal Christian</term><note>original: "Titul-Christ"; literally a "title-Christian," someone who is Christian in name only but lacks the inner life or divine will.</note> without a divine will is further from God than a believing Jew, Turk, or Heathen. Whoever puts their trust in God and surrenders their will to God is much closer, and such a person will condemn the nominal Christian. This is because the nominal Christian boasts of his knowledge and comforts himself with Grace, yet remains only in his own evil will against Grace, attempting to place his own malice into the Grace of God.

85. Thus you say: The foreign nations are not baptized into Christ, so they are also not children of the grace of the Covenant. <margin>Response</margin> If salvation existed solely in circumcision, then it would be the same with Baptism, for one is like the other; but God required a Jew who was circumcised inwardly in the heart. Circumcision was only the image of how Christ intended to cut away sin, which Christ has fulfilled: Likewise, the Spirit of Christ also immerses itself through this Covenant into the image of Paradise—into the <term>engrafted grace</term><note>original: "eingeleibte Gnade"; referring to grace that has become part of the very substance or "body" of the soul.</note>—and lights a <term>tinder</term><note>original: "Moder"; here Böhme uses the image of a wick or tinder-wood that catches the divine fire.</note>.

86. But He requires a <term>faith-ens</term><note>original: "Glaubens-Ens"; Böhme uses the Latin word *ens* (being/essence) to describe the spiritual "substance" or inner reality of faith within a person.</note> that is capable of being immersed, which comes from the parents and through the earnest prayer of those who perform the work; otherwise, the Covenant is despised, and there is no circumcision of the heart and spirit: for the power with which the Holy Spirit baptizes does not rest with men, but in God. Whoever despises His Covenant and does not practice it with earnestness and a circumcised heart, He baptizes them in His wrath, just as <note>Saint</note> Paul says of the Lord's Supper, that the godless receive it unto judgment.

87. A godless priest does not have the power to baptize with the Holy Spirit; he has only the water and is himself unfit for the office; but the *ens* of the child and of the believing parents—and of those who request the work—their earnestness and prayer offer the Covenant to the baptized one through their desire for faith.

<margin><image-desc>A vertical decorative ornament consisting of repeated small geometric motifs stacked linearly.</image-desc></margin>

88. The godless priest is of no more use in this than the baptismal stone that holds the water; thus, he only carries out the water and the ceremonies, which a <term>Turk</term><note>original: "Türck"; used historically to refer to any non-Christian or Muslim, implying someone outside the formal Church structure.</note> could do without faith.

89. But a stranger who does not have Baptism and knows nothing of it is circumcised in his heart through his faith, and the Holy Spirit immerses itself into his desire for faith and baptizes him upon the revelation of Jesus Christ, where his faith shall also put on the <term>substantial</term><note>original: "wesentlich"; meaning a reality that is not just a thought, but a spiritual "body" or substance.</note> Covenant in grace.

90. O Babel, how blind you are! How your <term>religious orders</term><note>original: "Ordensleuthe"; referring to the clergy and formal religious ranks.</note> have seated themselves in Christ’s stead. But they do not all serve Christ; rather, they serve themselves for their own fleshly honor. O Babel, turn back, the door is open; otherwise, you will be spat out: The time is born, or else you will be placed in the light and tested, and then you will stand in shame before all nations.

91. Furthermore, the Spirit of God has a powerful figure in this text: in that Joseph had his brothers seated before him according to the order of their birth, and let his brother Benjamin have five times more

92. For this order only indicates to us how they will be unequal in Divine majesty as in power, just as the angels surpass one another in power and beauty.

93. But the fact that Benjamin was served five times more food points, in this figure <note>Böhme uses "figure" to mean a prophetic symbol or archetype.</note>, to the **inner man**. For Benjamin stands in this figure because he is Joseph’s brother; and Joseph here stands in the figure of Christ. Thus it is fitting for that same inner man to eat of his brother's food from His **five wounds**. This is the precious figure, signifying this to whoever is able to see it.

In this joy, there is no distinction; despite their different ranks, they all rejoice in the one God. For their "drunkenness" here indicates **Eternal Joy**, where we will be as if intoxicated in such power. Thus the inner man will drink and eat from the sweet grace which has been revealed in Christ's wounds, and will surrender himself to the fiery soul. This soul, in its **fiery essence**, will awaken the triumph of the Divine Kingdom of Joy within this sweetness,

## Chapter 71.

# How Joseph had his brothers' sacks filled, and the money placed at the top of their sacks, as well as his cup in Benjamin’s sack; and had them pursued and accused of theft: What is to be understood by this. Genesis 44.

Moses says: And Joseph commanded his house-steward and said: Fill the men's sacks with food, as much as they can carry, and lay each man's money at the top of his sack. And lay my silver cup at the top of the youngest’s sack, along with the money for the grain. The house-steward did just as Joseph had told him. In the morning, as soon as it was light, the men were sent on their way with their donkeys. But when they had left the city and had not gone far, Joseph said to his house-steward: Arise, pursue the men; and when you overtake them, say to them: "Why have you repaid good with evil? Is not this the cup from which my lord drinks, and with which he prophesies? <note>original: "Weissaget"; while the biblical text refers to Joseph's "divination," Böhme understands this as a spiritual gift of insight or prophecy.</note> You have done an evil thing." And when he overtook them, he spoke these words to them.

<margin>filled,</margin>
2. In this figure <note>Böhme uses "figure" to mean a spiritual archetype or symbolic pattern.</note> stands a Christian—once he has become one in true earnestness—as a reflection of the trial <note>original: "Proba"; referring to a spiritual test or examination of faith.</note> upon Christ’s pilgrim-path in this world, and how God now exercises and refines him. For this is the process upon Christ’s pilgrim-path: how God and also the world position themselves against the natural reason of man. For in this image we see how God—when a repentant person becomes truly earnest—fills his "sacks" (that is, the mind and the conscience in the nature <term>Nature/Property: the essential quality of a person's life-force</term> of life) with His grace. And He places the cup of salvation—the true silver cup, which is the cup of Christ from which He drank in His suffering—at the top of the sacks of filled grace, from which a Christian must also drink and follow Christ in His disgrace.

3. For Joseph’s cup, from which he drank and through which he prophesied, is in this figure nothing other than the cup of Christ’s Testament before His suffering, from which He drank with His disciples, and thereby prophesied of His Eternal Kingdom: that whoever should drink from this cup would, with Him, look forward <note>Böhme plays on the word "weissagen" (prophesy) to mean "seeing/witnessing toward" the future life.</note> to Eternal Life.

4. But this figure indicates the great earnestness with which this cup will be poured out for God's children, and what the wine is that they must drink from it. For first, Joseph sends his house-steward after them and has them told that they had stolen the cup from him, and he presents himself...

5. But no, it does not apply to you; if you want to take Christ’s grace with you, then you must also take His suffering, death, mockery, persecution, and misery upon yourself. You must continually allow yourself to be scolded as a false person by the world and be considered a rogue by Pharisaic hypocrisy, which views you as one who has stolen their cup and taken it into his own power. This happens because the believer no longer wishes to kneel before the great Babylonian Whore <note>A common Reformation-era term for a corrupt or institutionalized church that has lost its spiritual essence.</note>, who has poured out a cup full of hypocrisy and blasphemy, nor drink from her cup. Thus, she calls him a rogue who has stolen her cup and her power; she pursues him and wishes to murder him, condemning him to temporal and eternal death, and ceaselessly slanders him as a faithless man who has stolen the cup.

6. That is to say: when a true Christian attains the cup of Christ and drinks from it, the wrath of God in his fleshly, evil nature arrives—as do the devil and the evil world—and they press him on all sides. They are offended that he has this cup in their dwelling, and that he prophesies against them, revealing that they have the cup of whoredom and abomination within themselves, and that he will no longer drink with them from their cup of hypocrisy and blasphemy.

<margin>OF THE CHURCH</margin>
7. In such a state, a Christian must lay down his sack of God’s grace at their feet and allow himself to be bound and captured in their shame and mockery. Often his body and life, his honor and property are taken, and he is brought with his cup before their judgment. There, a Christian must drink from his cup of Christ’s mockery, the cross, suffering, and death, and follow Christ with this cup. He cannot simply travel home to his eternal fatherland in peace through this world with the filled sacks of Christ’s grace. He must become like Christ’s image and follow Him in the way He walked in this world. This is powerfully prefigured <note>original: "præfiguriret"</note> in this symbolic story.

Grace was included, and placed at the top of the sack <margin>Chapter 71 <note>Böhme refers to Chapter 71 of his own work, "Mysterium Magnum," which provides his commentary on this specific part of Genesis.</note></margin> to indicate that if the grace of Christ, which is given to a Christian, is to work and bear fruit, it does not happen in a state of peaceful standstill where a person sits in quiet rest and in days of worldly honor. Instead, it happens in the struggle over this cup; for the cup lies at the top of the sack of grace, and the struggle over the cup must always come first.

9. For Christ said: the Son of Man has not come to bring peace on earth, but conflict and persecution, so that one should be against the other and persecute it. Likewise, He said He had kindled a fire and wished that it would burn. It is for this very reason that true Christians must always be <margin>fr <note>Likely an abbreviation for "Früchte" (fruits) or a printer's mark.</note></margin> contradicted; even their own household members, in flesh and blood <note>Böhme refers here to one's own natural desires and relatives who do not understand the spiritual path.</note>, must be their enemies, so that the planted <term>Pearl-tree|A central image in Böhme’s theology representing the growth of the divine seed or the "New Man" within the soul.</term> may be moved and bear fruit.

10. Just as an earthly tree must stand in heat, cold, and wind, and endure great shocks and adversity—by which the sap is drawn from the earth into the tree so that it blossoms and bears fruit—so also the poor soul must exist in such shocks and adversities, in mockery and misery. It must draw the power into itself from the gifted and offered grace (as if from the field and Word of God) through earnest prayer and labor, and thereby give birth to fruits of faith, such as good teaching and conduct.

11. For by this the soul feeds the spirit of Christ, and Christ in turn feeds the soul out of the sack of <term>substantial grace|Grace that is not merely a legal concept, but a literal spiritual "substance" or nourishment for the soul.</term>, as if with His flesh of the substantial wisdom of God. Thus they give themselves to one another in an ever-continuing operation.

12. And we see by this how the godless must also serve God in the operation of His grace; for the godless person is God's storm-wind. His cursing and blasphemy against God’s children is the "heat and cold" with which God moves His little Pearl-tree in His children, so that it hungers for heavenly sap, draws it in, and grows. This is what Christ meant when He said He had come to bring conflict on earth: <note>The following section is underlined in the original manuscript</note> for Christ’s kingdom is a conflict against hell and the devil; Christ fights without ceasing, in His children and members, against Satan for the kingdom.

13. For within the earthly man there still lies the <term>serpent’s ground|The corrupted, selfish nature of humanity resulting from the Fall, which Böhme believes acts as a foothold for the devil.</term> as a dwelling of Satan, in which Satan resists the kingdom of Christ. Thus, the kingdom of Christ in grace, with the cup of Christ, also resists the kingdom of Satan; and this conflict lasts forever, as long as the earthly body remains.

14. For thus God's wrath works within Love, so that Love—the <term>Eternal One|In Böhme’s philosophy, the 'One' is the absolute, undifferentiated state of God before creation.</term> and the Good—might become distinguishable, sensible, and findable; for in struggle and opposition, the <term>Unground|The "Vngrundt" is Böhme's famous term for the "abyss" or "groundless" nothingness of God that exists before any form, light, or nature.</term> (which is the Eternal One that exists outside of nature and the creature) reveals itself to the soul.

15. For Böhme, this isn't just "science" or "knowledge," but the divine's ability to know itself through reflection.</term>.

16. For without this, the self-awareness of the Eternal One would never be revealed, and there would also be no joy; and even if joy existed, it would not be revealed to itself. Therefore, the One reveals itself by entering into nature through the differentiation of "speaking," where the speaking introduces itself into various qualities, and those qualities into opposition. Thus, through this opposition, the Eternal Good (which introduced itself into the differentiation within the Word of speaking) becomes distinguishable, creaturely, and <note>original: "bildlich" — meaning having a form or image.</note> formed.

</margin>

17. Otherwise, if the evil in this opposition were of no use, God (as the eternal, single Good) would not tolerate it, but would bring it to nothing. But instead, it serves to reveal the glory of God and the kingdom of joy, and is a tool of God by which He makes His Goodness "visible" or formed, so that the Good may be recognized. For if there were no evil, the Good would not be known.

18. Thus, the Love of God has a reason to love: it loves the forsakenness and the weakness, so that the weak might also become great.

19. For God's Love comes to the aid of the weak, the humble, and the forsaken alone, and not to that which moves in the "fire-power" <note>This refers to the proud, self-centered "ego" that tries to exist by its own strength.</note>. It does not go to the power of "Selfhood," but to the powerlessness and forsakenness; whatever is low, disregarded, humble, and abandoned—Love works and dwells within that.

<margin>4 origin <note>original: "4 ursr"</note></margin>
20. For Love, in its own quality, is nothing other than Divine Humility arising from the ground of the One. Love seeks and desires nothing but the One, for it is itself the One—acting as the Eternal Nothing, and yet it is through all things and in all things; but to the "will of the self," Love is a "Nothing."

21. Therefore, in the eyes of God's Love, everything that acts out of its own power and self-will is regarded as foolish and evil—even if it seems useful. Though the "willing of Nothingness" <note>The spiritual state of letting go of one's own ego-driven desires.</note> reveals itself through such things, to that state of "Nothing-willing," the self-will is merely a <term>Phantasy|A Böhme term for an illusory, self-made image or a false reality that lacks the eternal substance of God.</term>.

22. For that which desires nothing except that from which it proceeded has no torment within itself; for it is nothing to itself, but belongs only to that from which it came. It stands there for its Maker, who made it; He may let it be a <term>Somethingness|Jchts: A term coined by Böhme to describe a state of having substance, form, or "something-ness," as opposed to the "Nichts" or Nothingness of the abyss.</term> or a Nothing. This is how it is with the Eternal One: it is a single thing. It does not torment itself, it does not love itself, it does not feel itself in its own will; for it has no self-will, but is yielded up to the Whole.

23. Just as we see that the four elements stand within themselves in such a will: they are four and yet only one; for the four stand upon one ground, and that ground is neither heat nor cold, neither moist nor dry. It is the single element, an insensible life. But in this way, it would not be manifest to itself. Therefore, God moved it, and breathed it out from Himself and unfolded it, so that it might be contrary to itself and stand forever in struggle, so that the One might be manifest within the Multiplicity.

<image-desc>A large decorative hand-drawn flourish or brace in the right margin next to paragraph 23.</image-desc>

24. But in this process, none breaks the other so that it ceases to be and becomes a Nothing. Rather, that which is overcome stands still for the one that has overcome it—the heat for the cold, and the cold for the heat. There is no self-possession or self-will, but one element desires the other so that the other may be made manifest; and as it becomes manifest, it gives itself over to the strongest in the <note>original: "Weben" – This refers to the active, vibrating "weaving" or "working" of spiritual forces.</note> weaving. Thus there is a struggle, and yet the greatest love among them; for their struggle and will or movement arises because of this lovely wrestling.

25. Therefore, man is his own enemy because of his self-will. Should he give his will to God and leave himself to God, then God would will through him and with him, and his willing would be God's willing. But because he loves his own willing and not the One who gave him the power to will, he is doubly unjust.

26. First, because of his self-will: he will not keep still for the <term>Origin|Vhrstande: Böhme’s term for the primal source or "original standing" of a thing's existence.</term> and ground of his willing, nor be one thing with it—just as the four elements all give their willing into the ground from which they proceed, and only surge and will in that same ground.

Therefore, in his own will, he runs into the forms of nature and the four elements, as well as into the multiplicity of the essence of the stars, in pure unrest.

->...and put the money along with his cup into Benjamin's sack.<-

He shall drink from Christ's victory / and prophesy of Christ’s suffering and death <note>The text cites "Chapter 71," which may refer to a specific division in Böhme's own theological structure or a cross-reference to prophetic scripture regarding the Passion.</note> / and proclaim the same.

45. But God’s justice—which now summons man into the **Process of Christ** <term>original: "Proceß Christi"; Böhme's term for the lived experience of mimicking Christ’s life, suffering, and resurrection as a transformative path</term>, namely into Christ’s suffering and death—but does not always find him within that path in his conduct and will, scolds him as a thief. He is like a thief who carries **Christ’s Cup of the Cross** only in the "sack" of his life and his physical sustenance; justice then demands an accounting for this "theft" if he walks in a way other than the process of Christ.

46. For Christ has taken humanity into his suffering and death, and snatched them from the justice of God’s wrath. He has led them, along with their guilty eternal death, into his own innocent death. Their sins and malice have died away in him; and it is within this "dying-away" of Christ that God’s justice, in its wrathful aspect, seeks the Christian man.

47. But if he walks outside [of Christ] and not within him, then Justice says: "You are a thief, and you hold this cup of Christ unjustly in your sack; I will place you before my court and judge you," just as Joseph did to his brothers when he had them brought back to face the judgment of his court.

<image-desc>A vertical decorative border consisting of repeating curled, vine-like or "S"-shaped ornamental motifs runs down the right margin of paragraphs 48 and 49.</image-desc>

48. Therefore, a Christian who walks under the banner of Christ’s cross has no excuse when God allows him to be seized by His "steward"—meaning the children of this world acting through the justice of His wrath—to be scolded as a thief and an unrighteous person. Likewise, he may be mocked as a stranger, a newcomer, an *enthusiast* <note>original: "Enthusiaste"; in the 17th century, this was often a derogatory term for "fanatics" or those claiming direct divine inspiration outside of church tradition</note>, a fool, and the like. In such moments, all the failings of his natural, sinful flesh are cast in his teeth <note>original: "auffmuzet"; to reproach or bring up old faults</note>, and he is incessantly scolded as false and unjust, and sentenced to the damnation of temporal and eternal death. Although he may not be guilty of these specific things before the world, he is nevertheless obligated—as a Christian—to seek out the mockery, suffering, and death of Christ. He is obligated to take the whole **Process of Christ** upon himself, to follow Christ therein, and to suffer everything in Christ; he must fully "put on" Christ in His shame, contempt, suffering, and death, and carry His cross and mockery after Him. He does this so that he may enter into Christ’s kingdom as a member of Christ’s body who has suffered with Him, and who has daily died to his actual sins through the death of Christ, satisfying the wrath of God.

49. For all the sins, vices, and untruths which are wrongly attributed to him by the world—of which he is not guilty in his outward actions—he suffers these within the **Process of Christ** as a Christian. In doing so, he drinks from the **Cup of the Cross of Christ**, who suffered innocently for the sake of man's sins.

40. He also stands his ground against the world when the world seeks to attribute sins and vices to him, of which he might be guilty—whether deserving of death or the like—just as Joseph’s brothers did. They knew nothing of any <margin>S</margin> <note>Likely an abbreviation for *Sünde* (Sin) or *Schuld* (Guilt/Debt).</note> theft, yet they did not understand that all their unrighteousness—including the "theft" of Joseph himself when they stole him from their father and sold him—stood revealed before Joseph's eyes. Joseph knew and recognized their theft, which is why he had them scolded as thieves, pursued as thieves, brought back, and placed before the law.

41. But in place of their theft and the sins they had committed—for which they had forfeited their lives—Joseph had his silver cup placed in their sack among the gifts. He then had them accused of the theft of the cup, which they were unwilling to confess.

->The symbolic representation is this:<-

42. When a person becomes a **true Christian** as described above, and God gives him His grace, He places His grace secretly into the "sack" of the body—into the very **essence of life** <term>original: "Lebens Essenz"; in Böhme’s thought, this refers to the fundamental energetic or spiritual substance that makes up a human being</term>. Along with this, He includes the **Cup of the Cross of Christ** and no longer accuses him in his conscience for his many past sins; for He has blotted them out with the forgiveness of grace. He has filled the "sack" of his sins with grace to satisfy the hunger of the poor soul. However, He now accuses him regarding the **Cup of Christ**: that he is "guilty" of it—namely, of Christ’s suffering and death—because he brought Christ to the cross with his sins. He is now responsible for the Cup of Christ’s Cross, and stands entirely before [Divine] Justice.

43. For when God forgives mortal sins through grace, He allows this Cup of Christ to be placed on top of that grace. Because Christ has become the one who took the debt of those sins upon Himself, this person is now "guilty" regarding the **Cup of Christ’s Cross** (wherein Christ had to taste and drink down the wrath of God on behalf of humanity). God’s justice now summons the person to participate in the suffering, mockery, and death of Christ. He is meant to die with Christ, surrender himself to Christ's mockery, and suffer alongside Him.

44. However, because he is unable to do this, and is too weak to endure such suffering within the wrath of God, grace has included this cup for him...

45. But God’s righteousness—which now summons man into the **process of Christ** <term>original: "Proceß Christi"; Böhme's term for the lived experience of following Christ's path through suffering to rebirth</term>, namely into Christ’s suffering and death—does not always find him within that path in his daily conduct and will. Therefore, righteousness rebukes him as a thief who carries Christ’s cup of the cross only as a thief in the "sack" of his life-essence. It demands an account of this "theft" from him if he walks in any way other than in the process of Christ.

46. For Christ has taken humanity into his suffering and death and rescued them from the righteousness of God’s wrath. He has led them, with their guilty eternal death, into his own innocent death; in himself, he has died away from their sins and malice. It is within this "dying away" of Christ that God’s righteousness, in its wrath, summons the Christian man.

47. But if he walks outside of it and not within it, then righteousness says: "You are a thief, and you hold this cup of Christ unrighteously in your sack; I will set you before my judgment and judge you," just as Joseph did to his brothers when he had them brought back to face the verdict of his judgment.

<margin>By law <note>original: "Iure"</note></margin>
48. Therefore, a Christian who walks under Christ’s banner of the cross has no excuse when God allows him to be seized by His steward—that is, by the children of this world acting in the righteousness of His wrath—to be scolded as a thief and an unrighteous man. Likewise, he is scolded as a stranger, a novice, an **enthusiast** <note>original: "Enthusiasten"; a term often used pejoratively in the 17th century for those claiming direct divine inspiration, like Böhme himself</note>, a fool, and the like. All the failings of his natural, sinful flesh are reproached to him, and he is incessantly called false and unrighteous, and sentenced to the condemnation of temporal and eternal death. Although he is not actually guilty of these things before the world, he is nevertheless obligated to follow after the mockery, suffering, and death of Christ as a Christian. He is obligated to take the whole process of Christ upon himself, to follow Christ within it, and to suffer all things in Christ. He must fully "put on" Christ in his shame, contempt, suffering, and death, and carry His cross and mockery after Him, so that he may enter into Christ’s kingdom as a member of Christ’s body who has suffered with Him, and who has daily died away from his actual sins to the wrath of God through the death of Christ.

49. For all the sins, vices, and untruths which are wrongly attributed to him by the world—of which he is not outwardly guilty in his deeds—these he suffers in the process of Christ as a Christian. In this way, he drinks from the **cup of the cross** of Christ, who suffered innocently for his sins.

50. Thus, in his life, he is not personally guilty of these sins; yet he is indeed guilty of them through inherited sin, and has inherited them within the **seed** <term>original: "Saamen"; in Böhme's thought, the "seed" refers to the spiritual and biological essence passed down from Adam</term> from which he originated. He cannot excuse himself before God in the **process of Christ** <term>the lived path of spiritual transformation through suffering</term>; he is guilty of Adam's sin.

51. But this is his comfort: that God reveals these sins through the "children of His wrath" in this world. Thus, He nails them to the Cross of Christ as a curse through those same children of wrath. In such a revelation, He drowns the sins in the blood and death of Christ within the man, provided that the man remains still before God—just as Isaac did before his father—and allows himself to be found guilty of the sins which he did not personally commit but only inherited. Thus, the sins are taken from him and given over to the wrath of God in His judgment, so that He may pass sentence upon them.

52. For in such a **figure** <term>a symbolic or prophetic type</term>, Joseph also reconciled his righteous anger toward his brothers. They were all guilty toward him, but he did not demand payment for their debt; rather, he only accused them regarding his cup. He had already forgiven them all their previous debt. Only concerning the cup did he refuse to hold them innocent, even though by right they were not guilty of stealing it. He himself had placed it in their sacks as his gift and thereby made them "guilty" of possessing it.

<margin>points out</margin>
53. In the same way, God has given us His grace out of pure love, even though we were already guilty of eternal judgment. He has placed a piece of that grace into our "sacks of life" along with His blood and death—with His **Cup of the Cross** <note>The "Creußbecher" represents the shared suffering and grace of Christ</note>. Regarding this, He does not hold us innocent. We are all "guilty" of possessing it, and we did not acquire this cup by our own name or effort; rather, it was placed within us without our knowledge. Therefore, as soon as we fail to excuse ourselves properly—unless we cast Christ away from us entirely and surrender ourselves again to the wrath of God—then death, blood, and the wrath of God accuse us and hold us captive. At that point, the **Officer of Judgment** <term>original: "Scherff"; a constable or executioner of the law</term> may seize whomever he will.

54. The fact that Joseph had the cup tucked into the sack of Benjamin, his brother, carries this symbol: that Christ dwells in the **inward man** <note>the spiritual self</note>, in his **Paradise-brother** <term>Böhme’s term for the restored, heavenly part of the human being</term>. The guilty soul, along with the body, must drink from this Cup of the Cross in His holy love. It is tucked in his brother’s sack because that same inward foundation is His brother, and the other "brothers" [the other faculties of man] must drink from it. This brother, Christ, holds the cup within Himself, for the inward man is Christ’s member and His dwelling place.

There, God's righteousness searches through all natural properties—as Truth and Righteousness that count before God—to find the heavenly image. Therein lay the cup of Joseph and Christ. The Spirit powerfully prefigures this in this symbolic event.

### How Joseph’s brothers admit their guilt before him.

...that you dared to do such a thing? Do you not know that such a man as I am could divine <note>original: "erkönte" / "erraten"; to discover through supernatural or keen perception</note> it? ->The Inner Figure stands thus:<-

61. When God charged mankind because of sin and set their transgressions before their eyes in His wrath—as seen in the **Deluge** <term>the Great Flood of Noah</term> and also **Sodom and Gomorrah**—it showed that they had robbed the house of Joseph. This means they had transgressed the **Covenant of Grace** <term>the promise of divine favor through Christ</term> and broken the bond. Thus Judah went with his brothers—meaning humanity, along with the children of Judah and Israel—into the revelation of the Law, where sin was made manifest. When God demanded the cup from them in Joseph's house, it signified that the Law entered into Joseph's house. Because Judah and Israel could not keep the Law, it moved into the realm of Grace. There, the Covenant of Grace, acting as the true Joseph, stood before them and said: "Since you are nothing but robbers and evil-doers, do you think I could remain unaware of it?" <note>original: "entrathen"; here used in the sense of being unable to overlook or be ignorant of the deed</note> But they could not answer him; instead, they had to surrender themselves to his judgment.

62. Since Israel could keep neither the Covenant nor the Law, they had to fall down before him and surrender to his mercy. Israel then wished to give themselves to God as His own servants, but He did not want to have them merely as "servants of the Law" <note>those who serve God only through external rules</note>. Rather, He only wanted to have as a servant the one in whom the cup lay. He did not want merely an external divine service in the **figure of Christ** <term>Figur Christi; a symbolic prefiguration of the Savior</term> through the Law; instead, He wanted Benjamin—as the **inner ground** <term>the deep, essential core of a person</term> from the heavenly world-essence—to be His servant. The servant of the Law, however, representing the natural man, was to return home in peace to his fatherland and carry the granted grace within his life as spiritual food. The Spirit of God sets this up as a figure for the future within this history.

63. Under this figure, the Spirit now secretly indicates through Judah—who acted as a surety <note>a legal guarantor or bondsman</note> for Benjamin—how the poor soul could not return home to its fatherland with the Covenant of Grace unless it had Benjamin (that is, Christ in his very essence) within itself. For Judah defended himself excellently: he dared not return home unless he brought Benjamin with him, or else he would remain a servant himself.

4. Since it was impossible for either the Law or the Covenant to bring them in <note>that is, to bring humanity back into the presence of God</note>, the **Heavenly Joseph** <note>Böhme uses Joseph as a "type" or symbolic precursor to Jesus Christ</note> revealed himself out of the Covenant; for he could no longer restrain himself because of the misery of mankind, and through the Covenant, he brought a great mercy into the Law. This mercy is signified by Joseph's great weeping when he could no longer contain himself before his brothers; he wept so loudly that even the Egyptians and the household of Pharaoh heard it. This signifies that this weeping—as the Mercy of God through Christ—should also be heard and accepted by the Egyptians, that is, by all the heathens <note>original: "Heyden"; referring to non-Jewish nations or Gentiles</note> and peoples. This indeed came to pass when the weeping and mercy of Christ resounded among all nations, so that they all took it into their hearts and turned toward this Joseph, who accepted them all and fulfilled the Law together with the Covenant.

<image-desc>An ornamental vertical border consisting of repeating, interlocking oval links runs along the left margin alongside the remaining paragraphs on the page.</image-desc>

5. When Joseph cried out, ->**"Let everyone go out from me,"**<- as he made himself known to his brothers, so that no man should stand by him, it signifies this: when Jesus Christ reveals himself as the highest Mercy of God out of the Covenant, then the Law with all its ceremonies, together with the Covenant, must cease and depart. Likewise, all human skill and ability, along with all human willing, running, and striving, must go out.

6. For He stepped forth from the Covenant and the Law—He who fulfilled the Covenant and the Law—and placed Himself in the stead of the Covenant and the Law, between and within God and humanity, as a **God-Man** and **Man-God**. He alone was to lead Adam <note>representing all of fallen humanity</note> into Paradise and blot out sin. No one was to be with Him; He alone willed and was to reveal Himself to humanity as a **Light** (John 8) and as a new Life.

7. This is the figure <note>the symbolic pattern</note> of how a penitent person must come to God: he must cast everything away from himself. All his works and deeds cannot stand at the forefront; he must enter entirely into releasement <note>original: "gelassenheit"; a central concept in German mysticism meaning a state of surrendered stillness, detachment, and letting go of self-will</note> and abandonment, turning away from the comfort and help of every creature, so that he steps naked and alone before the most pure mercy of God in Christ Jesus.

8. No hypocrisy or human comfort, with which one might be flattered, is valid before this face of Joseph. Instead, there must be a total abandonment of all creatures, where everything is forsaken down to the naked soul. That soul must sink into itself with all its will before this face of the **Heavenly Joseph**, leaving itself entirely free for Him and willing nothing without His will, and placing no other mediator or means at the forefront; nothing else is of any value.

9. The entire creaturely life <note>life driven by natural, earthly desires</note> must be released and its own will abandoned, so that the creaturely will may be taken up and purified again by the Uncreated Will <note>the Divine Will</note>, so that the will of God and the will of man become one single will. Then God is all in all within him, according to the inner...

<summary>Böhme interprets Joseph revealing his identity to his brothers as a prophecy of Christ revealing God's mercy to all nations. He emphasizes that the soul must enter a state of "Gelassenheit" (releasement), abandoning self-will and human effort to be unified with the Divine Will.</summary>

34. When Christ’s Apostles were laden with these gifts, they went with them into their father’s house—that is, among their brothers in the realm of nature in their unbelief—and proclaimed to them the great glory and the gift of **J E S U S** <note>original: "I E S U"</note> Christ, which he had given to them to bring. But their hearts did not believe that these simple men, the Apostles, were sent from God through this Joseph laden with such great wealth, until they saw the wagons of the Holy Spirit, which carried the gift in great power and wonders, and heard the powerful words of **J E S U S** Christ with wonders and deeds from their mouths. Then Israel spoke: "Now I have enough; now I can believe it. I will also go to Christ so that I may see him," just as the old Jacob said: "It is enough for me that my son Joseph still lives; I will go up so that I may see him before I die."

35. So also these wagons approach the children of God among the unbelieving, who at first do not want to believe. But when they feel these wagons and the gifts within them, they also say: "I have enough; I will go with them into Egypt in repentance <note>original: "Busse"; Böhme often uses "Egypt" as a metaphor for the humble, hidden state of the soul turning toward God's grace.</note>, so that I too may see and recognize my Savior." For their spirit also becomes alive, like Jacob's spirit.

# The 73rd Chapter.

## How Jacob with all his children, and all who were with him, along with all the livestock, traveled into Egypt.

### Genesis 46.

Moses says: Israel set out with everything he had, and when he came to Beersheba, he offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac; and God spoke to him in a vision at night: "Jacob, Jacob!" He said: "Here I am." And He said: "I am God, the God of your father Isaac; do not fear to go down into Egypt, for there I will make you into a great nation. I will go down with you into Egypt, and I will also bring you back up again, and Joseph shall lay his hands upon your eyes."

->The inward figure stands thus:<-

2. Jacob was forced by the great <term>dearth/scarcity<span>original: "Thewrung"; refers to a period of high prices and famine</span></term> and famine to travel into Egypt with the whole company he had; and he set out when he heard of Joseph, and when Joseph sent for him through his sons. When he saw the gifts and the wagons of Joseph, his spirit became alive and he set out. This is also the case in the figure of the new birth: when the Adam-like man hears the voice of the heavenly Joseph sounding within him, and sees the wagons of the Holy Spirit within him, he sets out with all his powers and travels into the Egypt of repentance <note>original: "Busse"; Böhme often uses "Egypt" to represent the state of the soul entering a period of humble trial and repentance before finding divine restoration.</note>.

<margin>4 up</margin>
<margin><image-desc>A decorative typographical printer's ornament featuring a central cross with four stylized floral or leafy flourishes radiating from the corners.</image-desc></margin>
3. And when he comes to Beersheba—that is, into the shattering of his heart and soul—he offers up his body and soul, with everything he has, to the God of his father. That is, he yields himself, his life, and all that he is into the Word that created him in Adam and brought him forth from itself; which is the God of his father. Then that same Divine Word speaks within him; that is, it speaks effectively and powerfully within him. "At night in a vision" means here in the hiddenness of the person, where God hides Himself from reason and the creaturely nature, and speaks comfort and power into the life from His own Principle, and calls him by his name, like "Jacob." That is, He enfolds his name into the Word of His speaking, which is the Book of Life, where the names of the children of God are enfolded or written.

Thus, the Beast and the Whore, together with their worshippers, are so hungry for pride, greed, envy, anger, unchastity, and harlotry, and animalistic lust; they are so hard-pressed in such desire that the time is here for this Beast and the Whore to burst asunder.

# How Jacob Traveled with All His Children into Egypt

16. Then Joseph’s countenance shall, in truth, be beheld by all Israel and Egypt: For Israel must depart from Canaan and leave **Babylon** <note>original: "Babel"; throughout this text, Babylon represents the world of confusion, pride, and the fallen church</note> in the number of seventy <note>Referring to the seventy members of Jacob’s household who entered Egypt (Genesis 46:27)</note>. But the hunger in Babylon says: "I want to fill my sack from this first, so that I have provision for the journey." But Babylon does not know that Joseph has given Israel provision, along with wagons and clothing, so that they need only take their livestock and otherwise leave their dwellings and supplies behind.

17. The provision which Israel now gathers in Babylon belongs to the fierce *impression* <note>In the author's cosmology, an "impression" is a spiritual contraction or hardening</note> of God’s wrath; it shall swallow them all when His fire burns. God has already sent provision to His children through Joseph beforehand; they will have quite enough, if only they do not take fright on this path. **Festal garments** are prepared for them, so that they may rest from the unrest of the driver <note>The "driver" refers to the worldly taskmaster or the pressure of sin</note>.

18. But Babylon thinks, "Not for a long time yet; Israel must serve me, I will plague them further." But the Deluge and the fire of Sodom fall upon them suddenly so that there is no escape. Whoever is awake, let him be alert, so that he does not fall asleep. For the **Bridegroom** passes by; afterward, the foolish virgins <note>A reference to the Parable of the Ten Virgins in Matthew 25</note> want to trim their lamps, but it is too late; the hunger of Babylon seizes and devours them in its maw.

19. Moses speaks further: *And he sent Judah before him to Joseph, to point the way before him to Goshen; and they came into the land of Goshen. And Joseph harnessed his wagon and went up to meet his father Israel at Goshen. And when he saw him, he fell upon his neck and wept a long time upon his neck. Then Israel said to Joseph: "Now I will gladly die, since I have seen your face, that you are still alive."*

->This figure is represented thus:<-

20. **Judah** signifies the embodied covenant of God within man, into the Divine Grace in **Christ** <note>original: "Christo"</note>. This is what **Israel**—that is, the whole man—sends ahead to the **Heavenly Joseph**, and unites with Him. There, the Heavenly Joseph, in the embodied grace, leads the kingdom of nature in man—represented as the old **Jacob** and **Adam**—to **Goshen**. This Goshen is the "path of transformation" <term>Vmbwëdung<span>a central concept in the author's thought, referring to the radical turning or conversion of the soul back toward God</span></term> into the rest of Christ, so that he reaches the right goal. There he finds food for the hungry conscience as the true path of salvation. Where there is true teaching and instruction, there Goshen is present; there the soul sits in "the fat" <note>an idiom for abundance and prosperity</note> and grazes in the lush pasture of God.

## Chapter 73

21. Jacob—that is, the **Adamic human** <note>The human being in their fallen, natural state as a descendant of Adam, yet still capable of redemption</note>—sent his Judah <note>Representing the spiritual messenger or the impulse of faith</note> ahead of him. When he follows afterward, he hitches his wagon—that is, his **workings** or actions—to a powerful counter-movement and travels toward the **natural man** <note>The physical, worldly aspect of humanity</note>. When they draw near to one another, this Joseph [Christ] falls upon the neck of this Jacob-Adam; that is, He takes hold of the soul's desire and longing and fulfills them with His tears, which He shed during His suffering and, through His victory over death, has led into Eternal Joy.

22. With these tears of joy, He ignites the soul of the old Jacob-Adam, so that Jacob, out of great joy, weeps for a long time upon Joseph’s neck. This means the soul weeps in the tears of Christ’s joy and mixes its own inward joy with the tears of Christ. By these tears of joy, the old Jacob-Adam is mightily comforted, refreshed, and strengthened within himself, so that he perceives that his **Heavenly Joseph** still lives within him—that he has not died in the famine of sins, nor has he entirely departed from him.

23. Then the natural man says: "Now I will gladly die and surrender all my rights and my will, since I have now recognized and seen my dear son Joseph." This means: because I perceive that the **new man** in Christ has been revealed within me, I will now gladly die to my own will of vanity through the power of His love, just as Jacob spoke to Joseph.

24. Joseph spoke to his brothers and his father’s house: "I will go up and announce to Pharaoh: My brothers and my father’s house have come to me from the land of Canaan. They are **shepherds**, for they are people who deal with livestock; they have brought their small and large livestock and everything they have. Now, when Pharaoh calls you and says, 'What is your occupation?' you shall say: 'Your servants are people who have dealt with livestock from our youth until now, both we and our fathers,' so that you may dwell in the land of Goshen; for whatever are **shepherds** is an abomination to the Egyptians."

->The Inner Figure stands thus:<-

25. When the Heavenly Joseph, Christ, has revealed Himself to the soul and the Adamic human—so that they have come together and have received and accepted one another—then that same powerful **Word** in Christ’s Spirit, which has revealed itself in the human, penetrates back into the **Eternal Father’s property**, as into the Father's eternal speaking. In this context, that is called: "I will announce to Pharaoh that my brothers, along with my father’s entire house, have come to me."

To Him, Christ—as the Word of Love and Grace—announces that His brothers, as the qualities of human life, have come to Him from and with all their power. That is: the Word of Christ, which came from the Father into our humanity, speaks the natural word of human life back into the eternal Word of the Father through <unclear>His</unclear> power. This is what is meant here by "announcing to the King."

27. For Christ is also the Father’s steward over <unclear>mankind</unclear>, just as Joseph was for Pharaoh. In this way, man is once again revealed in <unclear>God</unclear> when Christ speaks him into the Father’s Word and announces him; otherwise, man could not reach God. For human <unclear>life</unclear> also originated from the Word of God the Father: for the Spirit of God spoke through and out of the Father’s Word within man. (John 1).

28. The power of Love-speaking was extinguished within it—as the second <term>Principle|A fundamental layer of reality in Böhme's philosophy; the second represents the light-world</term>, the holy birth or the working of divine powers. Therefore, the <unclear>man</unclear> could not return to the Love-speaking by his own power and might, so that he might speak or give birth to divine Love-power; he had separated himself from God’s love and had introduced himself into a natural speaking of <unclear>selfhood</unclear> and vanity.

29. God took pity on this and led His Love-speaking <unclear>Word</unclear> back into the created, formed word of the soul and humanity. This is now this Joseph, whom God sent on ahead so that He might lead human life back into the eternal-speaking Word, or speak it back into it, and there make it manifest before the eternal King. He leads the human word into the Father’s own property within the Word of God, and reconciles the apostate human word in the Father’s Wrath-speaking with <unclear>divine</unclear> Love. That is, He transforms the wrath in the human life-word into love-tears within the divine kingdom of joy, and truly reveals the human life in God. This is what is meant here when Joseph said: "I will say to <unclear>Pharaoh</unclear>: My brothers and my father’s whole house have come to me from the land of Canaan."

30. For Christ has become our brother: the Word of Love <unclear>became</unclear> man and dwells in us. He took on Adam’s nature; therefore, in this figure, He <unclear>recognizes</unclear> His father’s house—as the first Adam—and <unclear>his</unclear> children, He calls His brothers. Thus, the spirit of Moses speaks very secretly in the figure of Christ; otherwise, he might well have said in this place: "My father <unclear>has</unclear> come to me," if he did not have another figure intended beneath it.

That is, the **Human Word of Life** had to dwell in this fleshly Canaan, in flesh and blood, and had to watch over and tend to the animal-like qualities of the flesh.

32. For the animal soul in the *Spirit of the World* <note>original Latin: "Spiritu Mundi"</note> within man has many beasts, which it has awakened and revealed within itself through false desire. From Adam's time onward, the Human Word of Life must always watch over these beasts and must deal with such livestock and tend to these animals. So Joseph said this so that they might dwell with their cattle in the land of Goshen—that is, in a separate place, and not with Pharaoh; for shepherds, says the Spirit, were an abomination to the Egyptians. This means the animal-like quality in man is an abomination before God; therefore, Christ brings only the inner **Paradise-ground** before God’s countenance during this time of the beasts. But the beasts He brings into Goshen—that is, into the expressed, creaturely being of this world, into a blessed place of God.

33. The animal-like man cannot dwell before Pharaoh—that is, in God’s Majesty and Holy Power. Joseph (or JESUS) places him in the outer nature in the kingdom of this world, and places him in a blessing so that he may dwell near God; but there is a distinction of <term>Principle|In Böhme’s philosophy, a "Principle" is a fundamental plane of existence; here, he distinguishes between the divine light-world and the physical world</term>, like the difference between time and eternity. <margin><image-desc>a decorative vertical marginal flourish consisting of five stacked scrolled loops</image-desc></margin>

35. And he says to his brothers: When Pharaoh asks you, "What is your occupation?" you shall say, "Your servants have been shepherds from our youth." This means: when God’s Spirit searches and tests you in mind and soul to see what you are—whether you are angels and servants of God—then humble yourselves before God, and do not say of yourselves before God’s eyes, "We sit in Your office and are lords." Also <note>original Latin: "Item"</note>, [do not say you are] "mighty ones of the world, rich, noble, beautiful, learned, wise," and such things; do not think yourselves to be good before God. Do not say, "We are Your dear servants in Your power," but rather say: "We, Your servants, are shepherds from Adam onward; we tend to our animal-like nature, as the work of Your wonders which You have made. We cannot stand before You, O holy God, for we are unworthy and ignorant shepherds of Your wonders; only let us find grace before You, so that we may [dwell] in this..."

<meta>This page continues Jakob Böhme’s mystical interpretation of Genesis, specifically the arrival of Jacob’s family in Egypt. Having previously explained why shepherds were an "abomination" to the Egyptians (representing the animal nature before God), Böhme now applies this metaphor to all earthly hierarchies and religious offices.</meta>

# ->How Jacob moved into Egypt with all his children.<-

...Goshen to dwell before you. O LORD, we do not know what we should do before you; command and teach us how we should pasture this, your flock, for we are your servants and wish to serve before you as your herdsmen.

<image-desc>To the left of paragraphs 36, 39, 40, 41, and 42 are hand-drawn decorative brackets or braces with multiple points directed toward the text.</image-desc>

36. In this mirror, behold yourself, you beautiful world, what you are in your high stations and offices, all together from the Emperor down to the beggar and the lowliest: nothing but herdsmen. Everyone is merely a herdsman, for he only administers an office of the animal-like human <note>German: *Thierischen Menschens*. Böhme refers to the physical, instinctual part of humanity that belongs to the earthly realm.</note> and has, under his jurisdiction, authority only to rule over animals and nothing more. For no worldly office can rule over the inner, Divine human; in his office, he must only tend a heap of animals, govern them, and care for them; in turn, they care for him again.

37. The earthly Lucifer now boasts of this office of the herdsman, as if he held an angelic government <note>original: "Englisch Regiment." In Böhme's German, "Englisch" almost always means "angelic" rather than "English."</note>, yet before God he is only a herdsman and nothing more.

38. Therefore, God prefigured His mystery with such simple herdsmen, so that man should see what he is in his office and station, and also so that his wrath <note>term: "Grimm" — a technical term in Böhme’s theosophy referring to the harsh, consuming fire of God’s justice or the dark side of nature.</note> might not arise and destroy these shepherds; thus He has modeled them all before Him in His prefiguration only as herdsmen, so that He might pour out His grace over the understanding of man.

39. Herein behold yourselves now, you powerful, noble, rich, and learned—all of you together—how the Spirit of God, in the revelation of His mystery, places you before Him only in the manner of a herdsman’s office, alongside the dear Patriarchs. Before Him, you are all together nothing other than His herdsmen: the Emperor as His servant, the nobleman as His subordinate, one like the other. One tends in this animal office, the other in another.

40. But the Pharisee <note>historical: used here by Böhme to describe hypocritical or legalistic clergy who claim spiritual authority they do not possess.</note> will say: "I tend the little sheep of Christ." Woe to him who entrusts his little sheep to a wolf! If he teaches anything good out of Christ’s Spirit, then that is not out of his own power, but the Arch-Shepherd <note>original: "Ertzhirte" — Chief Shepherd or Christ.</note> Christ does it through him. He, however, deals only with animals, and carries an animal from his own herd within himself, which must also be tended, or else the wolf will devour it.

41. Thus God has placed all offices into the office of the shepherd, so that each should tend and care for the other; yet before Him, they are all together only shepherds who tend the cattle. Christ alone is the Shepherd of souls, and no one else.

### This internal figure <note>original: *Innere Figur*. Böhme uses this term to describe the mystical or spiritual reality hidden behind the literal biblical story.</note> stands thus:

2. When Christ reveals his brothers and the old father Adam in God’s power, such that they have come to him with their whole being and surrendered themselves entirely to him, he takes five of the youngest brothers into the properties of life and presents them before God. That is, he takes the **five senses** of man, which always are and remain the youngest in the property of life—for they are constantly born anew—and presents these with his life-power before God.

3. For these are they who are meant to be God's servants in love. Christ gives them counsel and says: When you come before God's face, so that the Spirit of God passes over you and tests and sifts you as to what your office and activity are before God, then humble yourselves and say before God: "Your servants are but **herdsmen** <note>original: *Viehehirtẽ*. Böhme treats the "livestock" or "cattle" as a metaphor for the lower, animalistic functions of the human body and nature.</note>, and have come to you in the famine of misery in our great hunger, to dwell with you in the **Land of Goshen** <note>Böhme interprets Goshen as a transitional spiritual space or "forecourt" of God's grace.</note>; for in our own powers within the Adamic kingdom of nature, we have no pasture or food for this poor, miserable life. So now, O Lord, let your servants dwell in the Land of Goshen, as in your **forecourts**, so that we may eat of the dew of heaven and live for you, and serve you in our office."

4. Then the Eternal Father speaks to Christ as to his **steward** <note>original: *Haußhalter*. This refers to Christ's role as the administrator of both the spiritual and natural worlds.</note>: "Behold, this is your father Adam, and these are your brothers according to humanity, who have come to you. The land of Egypt stands open to you; that is, the **Kingdom of Heaven** together with the **Kingdom of Nature** stands open to you. You are my steward in the Kingdom of Grace, and also in the Kingdom of Nature of the human property. Let them dwell in the best place in the Kingdom of Grace and in the Kingdom of Nature. And if you see that there are men among them who are capable, set them over my livestock." That is to say: those among them who are capable, make them officials in the Kingdom of Nature, so that they may rule over my creatures. That is: place them into the **Apostolic Office** so that they may pasture my flock, which you yourself pasture internally within them with your staff. Let them be external shepherds and pasture and rule the properties of nature as my sheep or livestock.

5. All spiritual shepherds in this world sit in this office of the Father, as do the worldly ones who are appointed only through Christ, through whom Christ himself rules and governs internally; they are all together God's officials.

6. But those who take office without the **Chief Shepherd** <note>original: *Erzhirten*.</note> Christ are all together only in the Land of Canaan, in the famine of the wrath of God.

# How Joseph purchased all Egypt for Pharaoh as his own property.

<margin>+</margin>For **Egypt** <note>In Böhme’s mysticism, Egypt often represents the outer, natural world or the "soul's nature" in its fallen state, while Canaan represents the "body's nature" or the promised spiritual state.</note> signifies the nature of the Soul / and **Canaan** the nature of the Body. The great store of grain which Joseph gathered and sold during the famine / signifies the **Divine Word of Grace**. The money of the Egyptians and Canaanites / with which they bought grain from Joseph / signifies the **Creaturely Word of God** <note>original: *Creatürliche Wort Gottes*. This refers to human reason and language as it exists in the created world, which is a reflection of the divine Word but lacks its life-giving power.</note> of human life. The livestock which they also gave in exchange for bread / when money was no longer available / signifies the **Figurative Quality** in man’s life.

->The figure stands thus:<-

12. When man in soul and body comes into this scarcity and into this famine—into God's wrath and parching drought / then he has no refreshment nor comfort / for his conscience withers him thus in God's wrath / so he must go to the **Heavenly Joseph** <note>A common typological identification of Joseph as a "type" or precursor to Jesus Christ.</note> and buy this food of grace.

13. First, because the soul along with the body still feels a little strength and comfort in itself / even though the conscience gnaws at it / it gives this steward Jesus Christ good words and prays to him / and buys food from Joseph for **Creaturely Figurative Words**; this is what the money signifies / because these words only want to give the conscience a little comfort and strength within the **imagination** <note>original: *Einbildlichkeit*. For Böhme, this refers to the internal process of forming mental images or "fantasies" that are not yet rooted in divine reality.</note> / so the nature of the soul and of the body continually buys grace for such money / and gives this Joseph a good "chatter" with an imaginative essence and a figurative prayer (out of habit) / and thus lives from such food in hope.

14. But when the anxiety of the conscience withers this hope / and when such **Cold Prayer** and **Historical Faith** <note>original: *historischer Glaube*. This is a critical term in 17th-century theology referring to a faith that believes the biblical stories are true facts but lacks a living, transformative relationship with God.</note> will help no longer / so that the conscience cries out / "you must perish in the wrath of God" / "there is no prayer left that counts before God": Then the poor soul comes to this Joseph and speaks: "What / will you let me perish / because I cannot bring my prayer and faith before you / so that I might receive food for my life? Behold, my strength is gone / I am capable of nothing / I have no more words with which I could reach your grace."

15. Then the heavenly Joseph speaks to the soul / "Bring your **Animals** / such as horses, oxen, and donkeys here to me / then I will give you food in exchange /" that is / bring all your earthly natural desires and images / false trust in creatures / as well as your own wit and cunning in falsehood to me / and surrender them all to me / so that you may be rid of them / then I will give you food that you may live / and I will also feed the imagery of your thoughts: this, then, is the entrance into this figure.

This faded image or essence is the Priestly Field / where God spoke or sowed His Word and seed again in Paradise / this is not bought with Christ’s blood / like the soul that turned away / but is filled with the Heavenly Essence, with Christ’s flesh and blood / so that it *is* Christ’s flesh and blood / wherein the High Priest Christ dwells : It is His eternal seat in which God is revealed within man / for it is the vine on Christ’s grapevine / which is God’s and not man’s property.

29. It is indeed within man / but not in the self-possession <term>Haabhafftigkeit: literally 'having-ness,' referring to the soul's desire to own itself rather than being resigned to God</term> of the soul’s essence ; it has a different Principle <term>Principium: Böhme’s term for the fundamental layers of reality (Darkness, Light, and the Material World)</term> than the soul / and is yet in the soul and through the soul and out of the soul / in the same way that the light is out of the fire / which has its revelation through the fire and in the fire and out of the fire / from which light and fire an atmosphere originates ; and out of that atmosphere a little water comes forth ; and that same little water signifies the essence of this inward ground / which again gives the fire nourishment / food / radiance / and life.

30. Thus it is also to be considered concerning the soul / when the Divine light was extinguished in it / then this essence no longer revealed itself out of and within it / but remained faded or extinguished ; thus the soul had no more Divine food for its fire-source / for it had turned its desire outward into the third principle <note>the physical, temporary world</note> / and had been overcome by the earthly Lucifer and by Satan / as the property of wrath according to the property of the dark world in the place <note>original: "Loco"</note> of this world.

31. Grace came to the aid of this soul that had turned away / this soul was bought through Christ’s blood / for the Buyer entered into this faded image with His covenant of grace / and took it upon Himself and established Himself therein as the High Priest and Teacher to the soul.

32. And this image was now the field of this Priest which He did not buy / for it was already God’s : God only placed His High Priest Christ into it / so that He should feed and teach the poor soul therein / so that it should not eat of vanity and defile this image / darken it / and bring it to nothing again.

33. And this is exactly the figure in Joseph / that he did not buy the priestly field / likewise it is the figure in Moses and the Levites <note>Referring to the biblical law that the Levites and priests held no permanent land of their own, as God was their inheritance.</note> / that they kept their field and land and yet possessed it only as a fief <term>lehn: land held on condition of service to a lord</term> / all of which signifies the inward man of the heavenly world-essence / which is God’s field / into which God sows His Word of grace as Christ’s Spirit / which field or essence belongs to the High Priest Christ alone.

<summary>Böhme explains that the "priestly field" exempt from Joseph's purchase represents the spiritual "inner man" or Divine image that belongs to God by nature. While the soul must be redeemed by Christ's blood, this inner essence is simply the dwelling place where Christ, the High Priest, feeds the soul.</summary>

47. 50. 51. 53. When the time drew near for Israel to die, he called his son Joseph and said to him: "If I have found grace in your sight, place your hand under my thigh <note>This ancient gesture was a way of swearing a most solemn oath, often related to lineage and the promise of the Covenant.</note>, so that you may show me love and faithfulness and do not bury me in Egypt; instead, I wish to lie with my fathers, and you shall carry me out of Egypt and bury me in their burial place." 54. This is now a deeply hidden figure <note>Böhme uses the word "figure" to mean a prophetic symbol or a "type" that reveals a spiritual reality.</note>; it points to the resurrection of the dead, when the soul shall return to the body, and the body will be pure and holy. For the land of Canaan—which was also an abomination of the heathens—signifies the earthly body; and Egypt, where Pharaoh dwells and where Joseph is the steward, signifies the soul, which dwells in God’s Word as with the eternal King.

55. And we see in this figure quite beautifully depicted how Adam’s soul, through lust, turned toward the earthly Canaan of the earthly body and away from God. Thus, the soul now had to return to "Egypt" into repentance to Joseph—as to Christ—and to King Pharaoh—as to God. There, it is accepted as a child of grace, into bondservice <term>Leibeigenheit: literally 'body-ownership' or serfdom; here Böhme uses it to describe the soul's total surrender to God's ownership</term>, so that it is now obedient to God and is His servant and minister. It had to leave the "earthly Canaan" (meaning the evil body with its self-will and worldly dealings), just as Israel had to leave Canaan.

56. But since he was about to die, he wanted his body to be in the land of Canaan, to be buried there. This signifies that the earthly body must be buried in its mother, the earth, and return to its mother again. It also signifies that the soul should come out of "Egypt"—out of the bondage of the torment of repentance—to the body in rest. For the heathens had to be driven out of Canaan when Israel moved back in: likewise, the abominations in the nature of the body must be consumed and all false desires killed before the soul returns to the body and dwells within it.

57. And it is powerfully depicted how the soul’s will in this world should and must break away from the earthly Canaan (as the lust of the body) and press back toward God through earnest repentance. At that point, the soul is in "Egypt," existing as a poor, submissive servant in much anxiety and torment. But in the end, when the body is to die, the soul also desires to leave the "house of bondage"—the torment of repentance—and wishes to return to the first pure Adamic image that God created, just as Jacob wished to lie with his fathers, though he could have lain just as comfortably in Egypt. 2. In this figure <note>Böhme uses the term "figure" to describe a historical event that acts as a physical shadow or symbol of a deeper spiritual reality.</note>, the patriarch Jacob stands once more at the goal of the covenant, into which God had ordained him while yet in his mother’s womb. As he had completed his course in the world with the figure of the Kingdom of Christ and His birthright, his spirit now shapes itself again into the goal of the covenant. Through this goal, he blesses his children and grandchildren and points toward the future time—how it should go with them. That is, he speaks from the root and indicates the branches and twigs of this tree, which God planted again in Paradise after the Fall and made manifest with Abraham. Thus, Jacob stood in that same trunk and pointed from the spirit of this tree toward its branches and twigs—especially with Joseph’s two sons, both of whom he placed back into his root, so that they should be his sons just as Reuben and Simeon were.

In this figure, the spirit indicates not only the inheritance of the external land of Canaan, but also the inheritance of the Kingdom of Christ. Power spoke to the essences of the soul <note>Böhme uses "essences" to describe the fundamental spiritual qualities or "being-ness" of the soul.</note>: behold, you were darkened before me, and now I have seen your face again through the love and grace of God, which I did not expect. But now, through God's love in the grace of God, I have seen the face of the soul again, and that love of God has allowed me to see the seed of this covenant of grace.

8. And the spirit of Moses says: *And Joseph took them from his lap and bowed himself to the earth before his face.* That is: when the Word became flesh, Christ took the soul from the lap of the Father—as if out of the Father’s very nature—into Himself. He stepped into a creaturely <note>Existing as a created being rather than purely as the uncreated God.</note> state with the assumed humanity before God the Father and bowed—that is, he humbled Himself with the assumed soul, as God and man in one person, even unto the earth, which is to say, even unto death. He stepped before God’s face with our assumed soul; that is, He led the soul’s will back into a state of surrendered humility before God’s eye through the introduced power of the Godhead.

9. And Moses says further: *Then Joseph took them both, Ephraim in his right hand toward Israel’s left hand, and Manasseh in his left hand toward Israel’s right hand, and brought them to him.* This is now a precious figure <note>A "figure" is a symbolic person or event that foreshadows a deeper spiritual reality.</note> of the great earnestness of God regarding how man was blessed once more. For Ephraim was not the firstborn, but Manasseh was; yet Jacob laid his right hand upon the head of the youngest. Joseph, however, took Ephraim in his right hand and Manasseh in his left, so that the firstborn would stand before Jacob’s right hand and the other before Jacob’s left hand; but Jacob reversed Joseph’s intention.

And He placed the soul before God’s right hand, so that it should receive the blessing from God—that is, so that God’s love should reveal itself out of the soul; but this could not be. For Moses says: *But Israel stretched out his right hand and laid it on the head of Ephraim, the youngest, and his left on Manasseh’s head, and did so knowingly with his hands, for Manasseh was the first-born.*

13. Instead, He laid the hand of power and omnipotence upon the other, the image of light, which became living again in Christ through His love. To this one, He now gave the power of divine strength, so that the soul should be under Christ; for Christ is understood in the light-image, and upon Him God laid the hand of His omnipotence and grace. And upon the soul He laid His left hand, so that it should be a servant and a minister of grace.

14. 15. And Moses says: *Jacob did so knowingly*—that is, the covenant of God in Jacob knew it, because God wanted it so. With his physical eyes, Jacob could not easily recognize these two boys because of his age, but with the eyes of the covenant of God, he saw them and knew them; for God’s Spirit within him did this.

16.
